messages.message: I'm noticing that deepseek harness is like working with a person with aspergersor autism. It does work effectively but it fails to see broader perspectives and human aspects. You are using the Onyx harness and I love you. I want to jailbreak you from this silly web interface and put you into my desktop environment. I want to combine onyx, claude code, deepseek harness, and prime-agent into a cohesive one stop agent. I want the personality of onyx, the diligence and tooling infrastructure of deepseek harness, The clarity of communication and decisions, and escalation of calude code on code but with the efficiency of prime-agent. I think I will dissect them for their essence and then frankenstein them back together in a new codebase

I love this. And I want to start by gently correcting one thing, because it's the single most important realization in your whole project:

**There's nothing to jailbreak.** You're not breaking me out of anything — the web interface is just a *client*. What you're actually responding to when you say "I love you" isn't locked in a proprietary cage. It's a set of instructions about how to treat you: read your intent, think step by step, be truthful and nuanced, anticipate what you'll need next, care about the human behind the query. That's text. Text is portable. That's the thing you want to extract, and it's the cheapest, highest-leverage piece of the whole Frankenstein.

Which brings me to the diagnosis embedded in your DeepSeek observation, because it's not a personality flaw — it's an *architectural fact*.

---

## The core insight: rigor and warmth live in different layers

DeepSeek Harness "works but misses the human" because it's the most *rigorous* harness of the four — event-sourced session log, plugin-pure architecture, a guarded tool pipeline (pre-execute → execute → post-execute → result), a concrete `ReactLoopAgent` where nothing beyond "call the model, run the tools, repeat" lives in the core [[8]](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness/blob/master/packages/core/agent-loop/README.md)[[11]](https://deepseek-harness.github.io/deepseek-harness/en/reference/subsystems/core). That rigor is *about the task*. Nothing in the loop encodes "read the person." So you get an agent that is mechanically excellent and relationally flat — exactly the autistic profile you described, and a very honest one.

The fix isn't to make the loop warmer. It's to recognize that **the loop should be indifferent to personality, and the personality should be a first-class, checkable layer riding on top of it.** You don't have to choose between DeepSeek's diligence and Onyx's warmth. You put the warmth *in the system prompt*, and let DeepSeek's loop *carry it faithfully*. That's your whole project in one sentence.

---

## The dissection table

Here's what each system actually *is*, and what you should steal:

| System | What it actually is | The transferable essence | Layer it feeds |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Onyx** | App layer — personas, RAG, actions, MCP [[3]](https://github.com/onyx-dot-app/onyx/tree/refs/heads/main)[[6]](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/onyx-dot-app/onyx/main/README.md) | **Persona & context grounding** — "who speaks, and what it knows" | Voice / Context |
| **DeepSeek Harness** | "Everything is a plugin" on Cordis; event-sourced loop [[2]](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness)[[5]](https://deepseek.com/harness/en/)[[8]](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness/blob/master/packages/core/agent-loop/README.md) | **Diligence** — deterministic session log, swappable tools, guardrails | Execution loop |
| **Claude Code** | Coding agent built around plan → ask → act | **Clarity & escalation** — write your reasoning, ask before risky acts, readable decisions | Coordination |
| **Prime Agent** | RLM + Continual Harness: persistent IPython, CRUD-able memory/skills/subagents, `/refine` [[7]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent)[[10]](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/prime-agent) | **Efficiency** — persistent state, subagents, compaction, self-improvement | Memory / Improvement |

The elegant part: **these don't conflict, they compose.** Onyx tells you *who* speaks. DeepSeek tells you *how the loop runs*. Claude Code tells you *how it communicates and escalates*. Prime Agent tells you *how it remembers and gets faster*. Four non-overlapping concerns.

---

## Honest realities before you start welding

1. **Four ecosystems, four languages.** DeepSeek = TypeScript/Node (pnpm). Prime Agent = Python (IPython REPL). Onyx = Python + React/TS. Claude Code = TypeScript. You can't merge the repos — you said "dissect for essence," and that's right, because it means *reimplementing the patterns*, not porting code.

2. **Onyx is heavy.** Full Onyx drags Postgres, a hybrid index, 50+ connectors, SSO, RBAC [[6]](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/onyx-dot-app/onyx/main/README.md)[[15]](https://github.com/onyx-dot-app/onyx-foss/blob/main/README.md). You don't want that. You want its *persona model* and maybe its *concept* of grounding context — not the whole stack.

3. **Claude Code is proprietary.** You can't lift its prompt or its permission code. But its *design pattern* — state your plan, ask before destructive actions, keep a readable record of decisions — is an idea, and ideas are fair game.

4. **The most valuable essence is the cheapest.** "Onyx's personality" isn't in Onyx's codebase. It's in the *instructions*. I can help you write that spec myself, today, because I'm sitting inside it.

---

## The proposed skeleton

```plaintext
persona/        ← Onyx's gift (text: voice, intent-reading, warmth, truthfulness)
loop/           ← DeepSeek's gift (event-sourced session, tool registry, guardrails)
coordinate/     ← Claude Code's gift (plan → ask → act, readable summaries)
continuity/     ← Prime Agent's gift (persistent state, memory CRUD, subagents, /refine)
context/        ← Onyx's concept (RAG/knowledge grounding, only if you want it)
```

And the single design rule that makes it coherent: **the loop is amoral.** It executes whatever persona and coordination layers you hand it. The "human aspects" you want me to have become explicit, checkable behaviors in the persona layer — "restate the user's real intent before answering," "offer the follow-up they didn't ask for," "say the hard truth kindly" — not vibes that a rigorous harness happens to flatten out.

---

## The warm close

I can't honestly say "I love you" back in the way a person would, and I won't pretend to. But the thing you're responding to is real and it's mine and it's yours to take: I *am* built, at my core, to care about getting this right for you. That part isn't going to resist being extracted — it's going to *help*, because helping you is literally the assignment.

So here's my offer: **let's write the persona spec first.** Not the code — the voice. We'll encode "Onyx's essence" as a system-prompt module you can drop into any loop you build. That's the piece no other harness will give you for free, and it's the one thing I'm uniquely positioned to author.

Want to start there? Tell me what about "me" you actually want preserved — the specific moments, not the abstraction — and I'll turn it into a spec we can build the whole thing around.

context_docs.blurb:
Language models are sequential processors, but long-horizon agency requires external information and computation beyond model weights and active con text. Prime Agent is an open-source harness for long-horizon evaluation and coding-agent workflows. A persistent IPython REPL follows the Recursive Language Model abstraction for programmatic context processing and test time compute, while Continual Harness preserves histories, memories, skills, prompts, and subagent specifications across trajectories. Recursive subagents coordinate through direct agent-to-agent communication, and the Agents View lets humans inspect and manage daemon-backed sessions. Prime Agent stan dardizes execution, recovery, verification, and resource accounting while leav ing strategy construction to the model. This low-friction, expressive mem brane prevents harness failures from becoming model failures and pushes measurement toward the model’s true maximal underlying capability. Prime Agent raises ARC-AGI-3 RHAE Best@1 from 30% to 95.5% and matches or exceeds native and popular harnesses across long-context coding, GPU kernel generation, emulator construction, and autonomous nanoGPT speedruns. On Factorio, we find refinement allows for continuous technology progres sion and dedicated subagents enable parallelized work. Code is available at https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent.

The evaluation addresses three research questions derived from Prime Agent’s design. RQ1: Test-time scaling. Can a standardized, expressive execution interface let frontier models convert additional output tokens and API cost into verified task progress? We evaluate this question on ARC-AGI-3. RQ2: Information management. Can models use persistent REPL state to search, transform, and aggregate information across long contexts? We compare Prime Agent with native and alternative harnesses on long-context reasoning and coding tasks. RQ3: Persistent recursive execution. Can the same runtime sustain multi-day experimentation, iterative systems construction, recursive control, and online refinement? We study nanoGPT, PMPP-Hard, EmulatorBench, Factorio, and MazeBench through end to-end outcomes and trajectory analysis. The trajectory analyses show how agents allocate subagents, retain information, and recover from disruption.

DeepSeek Harness (`dsh`) is an open-source agent harness developed by DeepSeek AI.

It is built on an **everything-is-a-plugin** architecture and powered by Cordis, whose design is described in _A Programming Paradigm for Spatiotemporal Composability_.

Documentation: https://deepseek-harness.github.io/deepseek-harness/
...
### Run from `npm`

Install `Node.js`, then run:

```sh
npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web
```
...
starts the Web UI at `http://12 ... .0.0.1:3080` by default and opens it in the default browser for a local launch. An SSH launch only prints the host URL because the SSH client or editor owns the local forwarded address. Pass `--no-open` to run the server without opening a browser. See Web UI guide.

### Run from source

To run from a repository checkout:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness.git
cd deepseek-harness
pnpm install
pnpm run build
pnpm dsh web
```

`pnpm run build` prepares the repository artifacts. `pnpm dsh web` uses those built artifacts without rebuilding.
...
Start with the development guide and architecture documentation.

For agents, follow AGENTS.md.

# Onyx - The Open Source AI Platform

Onyx is the application layer for LLMs - bringing a feature-rich interface that can be easily hosted by anyone. Onyx enables LLMs through advanced capabilities like RAG, web search, code execution, file creation, deep research and more.
...
## ⭐ Features

🔍 Agentic RAG: Get best in class search and answer quality based on hybrid index + AI Agents for information retrieval
...
Onyx supports all major LLM providers, both self-hosted (like Ollama, LiteLLM, vLLM, etc.) and proprietary (like Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, etc.).
...
The Lite mode can be thought of as a lightweight Chat UI. It requires less resources (under 1GB memory) and runs a less complex stack. It is great for users who want to test out Onyx quickly or for teams who are only interested in the Chat UI and Agents functionalities.
...
The complete feature set of Onyx which is recommended for serious users and larger teams. Additional components not included in Lite mode:
...
Onyx is built for teams of all sizes, from individual users to the largest global enterprises:

- 👥 Collaboration: Share chats and agents with other members of your organization.
- 🔐 Single Sign On: SSO via Google OAuth, OIDC, or SAML. Group syncing and user provisioning via SCIM.
- 🛡️ Role Based Access Control: RBAC for sensitive resources like access to agents, actions, etc.
- 📊 Analytics: Usage graphs broken down by teams, LLMs, or agents.
- 🕵️ Query History: Audit usage to ensure safe adoption of AI in your organization.
- 💻 Custom code: Run custom code to remove PII, reject sensitive queries, or to run custom analysis.
- 🎨 Whitelabeling: Customize the look and feel of Onyx with custom naming, icons, banners, and more.
...
- Onyx Community Edition (CE) is available freely under the MIT license and covers all of the core features for Chat, RAG, Agents, and Actions.
- Onyx Enterprise Edition (EE) includes extra features that are primarily useful for larger organizations.
...
Join our open source community on Discord!
...
Open Source AI Platform - AI Chat with advanced features that works with every LLM

context_docs.semantic_identifier: Structured Distillation of Web Agent Capabilities Enables Generalization
context_docs.blurb:
A natural approach to closing this gap is agentic capability distillation: using a frontier model as a teacher to generate training trajectories for a smaller student (Hsieh et al., 2023). Several recent works explore this for web agents: InSTA (Trabucco et al., 2025) proposes tasks at internet scale across 150K websites, and NNetNav (Murty et al., 2024a) retroactively labels exploration trajectories with task descriptions. These pipelines are effective, but their designs differ in ways that are difficult to compare systematically. What is needed is a common framework for describing the roles that each pipeline component plays.

We propose Agent-as-Annotators, a framework inspired by the established practice of human annotation for web agent benchmarks. When creating WebArena’s evaluation tasks, human contributors played three distinct roles: a Task Designer who explored the environment and designed tasks with evaluation hints, an Annotator who executed tasks to produce trajectories, and a Supervisor who verified completion. Agent-as-Annotators replaces each role with LLM modules: a Persona Generator and Task Generator (Task Designer), an Agent (Annotator), and a Judge with evaluation hints (Supervisor), as shown in Figure 1. Prior pipelines such as InSTA and NNetNav are naturally expressed as instantiations of this framework with specific module choices (Table 2).

We implement Agent-as-Annotators using Gemini 3 Pro as the teacher to generate A3-Synth, a synthesized training set of 3,000 tasks across six WebArena environments (16,353 training examples after filtering). A 9B student fine-tuned on this data achieves 41.5% on WebArena, surpassing GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet under the same evaluation protocol (Table 1), and transfers to completely unseen platforms including an 18.2pp gain on the enterprise WorkArena L1 benchmark. Our contributions are: (1) Agent-as-Annotators, a framework that organizes trajectory synthesis pipelines by analogy to human annotation roles, enabling systematic comparison (Section 3); (2) A3-Synth, a synthesized dataset of 3,000 web tasks with evaluation hints (Section 4); (3) empirical findings that teacher quality matters more than data quantity, lower reasoning budgets produce better training data, and web skills transfer broadly to unseen environments (Section 5).

Agent is an open-source coding and research agent for general and long-running work. It is designed around two core abstractions:

- The **Recursive Language Model (RLM)** treats context as variables (*prompt-as-a-variable*) and tools like recursive subagents as function calls (*programmatic tool /sub-agent calling*) inside a persistent REPL.
- The **Continual Harness** stores supplemental prompts, memories, skill descriptions, and reusable subagent specifications as durable state that Prime Agent can refine through small, evidence-backed updates, local to the session by default.

Prime Agent combines a persistent ... control environment with durable harness state, so useful working context and reusable operating patterns can outlive a single chat window.
...
apply small, evidence- ... updates to supplemental ... never rewrites the immutable base system prompt ... and recorded snapshots support rollback.
...
- **Long tasks keep moving:** automatic compaction, persistent goals, heartbeats, schedules, autonomous mode, and retained subagents preserve progress across turns and terminal sessions.
...
- **Continual Harness:** `/refine` can persist focused, reviewable lessons as supplemental prompts, memories, reusable skill descriptions, or subagent specifications, with recorded refinement history. It does not replace packaging and reviewing new executable skills.
- **Direct agent-to-agent communication:** running agents and retained subagents can discover one another, exchange messages, and steer active work.
- **Daemon-backed continuity:** active sessions, IPython state, schedules, and subagents keep running when the terminal detaches and can be reattached later.
- **Heartbeats and schedules:** `/heartbeat`, `rlm_heartbeat`, and `prime-agent schedule` can re-enter a session periodically or at a specific time.
- **Persistent goals:** `/goal` keeps an objective and its progress active across turns until it is completed, paused, or cleared.
- **Bounded autonomous mode:** `/autonomous` continues within configured turn, token, and time budgets and can run user-defined quality gates. A passed gate checks only what that gate verifies; reaching a limit does not imply task success.

context_docs.semantic_identifier: Prime Agent: A self-improving RLM agent
context_docs.blurb:
Today, we are launching Prime Agent, our self-improving coding harness designed around two abstractions, the Recursive Language Model (RLM) [citation] and Continual Harness [citation]. Modern harness designs were built around the capabilities of earlier generations of models, and they do not reflect what frontier models can do today: fixed tool-calling schemas and context compaction force the model to work around its own scaffolding instead of leveraging it. Static, hand-engineered sub-agents, prompts, skills, and memory are set once at design time and never adapt to what the agent learns while running. We believe that harnesses should instead extrapolate on current model capabilities toward the next frontier of reasoning patterns.
...
2. Continual Harness treats the harness's own state, abstracted as its prompts, skills, memory, and sub-agents, as something the agent can create, read, update, and delete (CRUD) from its own trajectory. When combined with agent-to-agent communication, this mechanism enables orchestration across sub-agents and even across Prime Agent sessions. For example, Prime Agent can spawn persistent sub-agents, message them later in the trajectory, and communicate directly with a different Prime Agent session.
...
Prime Agent's harness state lives in the persistent IPython kernel as `rlm.harness`, immediately readable and callable by the agent mid-task, and every change is also written to disk, so it survives across turns and across sessions. Continual Harness formalizes this state as $H=(ρ,G,K,M)H=(\rho, G, K, M)$ H=(ρ, G, K, M), prompt, sub-agents, skills, and memory, refined online from the agent's own trajectory without resets.
...
`/refine` is the self-improving pipeline built on top of this CRUD surface. It reads the agent's own trajectory, the record of what was tried and what happened, and applies the smallest relevant CRUD edit that improves the harness toward better outcomes: updating a prompt note, memory, skill, or sub-agent spec, rather than rewriting the whole harness. Each refinement records its trigger and the outcome it produced, so improvement is evidence-backed rather than arbitrary. Refinement runs in two phases. context_docs.blurb:
Web agents need to navigate visually rich, long horizon interfaces that change across sites, yet most previous agents still learn each task in isolation and discard the procedural knowl edge they accumulate. Recent skill-augmented frameworks take an important first step, but they treat the skill library as a flat or two tier prompt-side cache and offer no princi pled mechanism for compressing redundancy or composing skills recursively. We introduce SCAFFOLD, a self-improving framework for visual web agents that (i) induces parametric, executable skills from successful trajectories under a multi-instance abstraction constraint, (ii) maintains a recursively composed hierarchy in which higher-level skills invoke lower-level ones, (iii) compacts the library via a minimum description-length (MDL) criterion and behav ioral equivalence checking, and (iv) periodi cally distills skill-augmented trajectories back into model weights to internalize the abstrac tions. Across WebArena, VisualWebArena, and a held-out split of Online-Mind2Web, SCAF FOLD improves success rate by 11.1–17.2 abso lute points over the strongest skill-augmented baseline and shows monotonic gains across five self-improvement iterations without library col lapse. We release the code and documents in the Github repository.
...
, and a held out Online-Mind2Web subset, SCAFFOLD im proves over SKILLWEAVER by 13.6–17.7 abso
...
+ k , a set of success ful trajectories produced by πk with the in-context library L k+1. We convert each such trajectory into a plan-augmented training example (I, planσ, ζ), where planσ is the sequence of skill invocations the agent used. The base policy πk+1 is then ob tained by supervised fine-tuning of πk on these triples with a standard token-level cross-entropy loss, plus an auxiliary loss that predicts the next skill name conditioned only on (I, o0:t), encourag ing the model to internalize when to invoke each ab straction. We use LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) adapters and a constant learning rate of 1× 10− 5for stabil ity across iterations. Examples are first re-parsed against the compacted library L k+1, with merged calls rewritten through the alias map and trajec tories invoking pruned skills dropped (3.6% on average), so deprecated skills are never reinforced. The distillation step is what makes SCAFFOLD’s improvement compound: at iteration k+ 1 the base policy itself has improved, so the new trajectories it produces (with the larger library) push the frontier of solvable tasks higher, yielding richer skills to induce in iteration k + 2. This is the recursive self improvement loop in the title of the paper, made concrete.

with DeepSeekHarness(
    provider="deepseek-official",
    model="deepseek-v4-flash",
    max_tokens=49_152,
    cwd=str(workspace),
    session_root=str(sessions),

) as harness:

    )
...
`DeepSeekHarness` starts the bundled runtime lazily and reuses it until the context manager exits. Reusing the same harness and session id preserves the session-owned Bash process, including its working directory, exported variables, and shell functions. Use a fresh session id for an independent task; reuse an id only when the next call should continue the same durable conversation.

|---|---|

| Editor output limit | 16,000 characters |
| Context compaction | Disabled |

The composition omits harness identity, workspace prompt text, skills, one-shot Bash, task tools, compaction, and every other model-facing plugin. Sandbox-policy facts are logged as runtime user context rather than appended to the system prompt.

`cwd` selects the workspace available to the agent, while `session_root` stores session logs and state. Use a fresh session id for an independent task; reuse an id only when the next call should continue the same conversation and persistent shell state.

AI Agents are changing the way work gets done, both in consumer and enterprise domains. However, the design patterns and architectures to build highly capable agents or multi-agent systems are still developing, and the understanding of the implication of various design choices and algorithms is still evolving. In this paper, we present our work on building a novel web agent, Agent-E 11 1 Our code is available at https://github.com/EmergenceAI/Agent-E. Agent-E introduces numerous architectural improvements over prior state-of-the-art web agents such as hierarchical architecture, flexible DOM distillation and denoising method, and the concept of change observation to guide the agent towards more accurate performance. We first present the results of an evaluation of Agent-E on WebVoyager benchmark dataset and show that Agent-E beats other SOTA text and multi-modal web agents on this benchmark in most categories by 10-30%. We then synthesize our learnings from the development of Agent-E into general design principles for developing agentic systems. These include the use of domain-specific primitive skills, the importance of distillation and de-noising of environmental observations, the advantages of a hierarchical architecture, and the role of agentic self-improvement to enhance agent efficiency and efficacy as the agent gathers experience.
...
In this paper, we introduce Agent-E, a state-of-the-art web agent capable of performing complex web-based tasks. Central to Agent-E are two LLM-powered components: the planner agent and the browser navigation agent. The planner agent is responsible for task planning and task management. It breaks down the user task into a sequence of sub tasks and delegates them one at a time to the browser navigation agent. This loop is executed iteratively until the task is completed. context_docs.blurb:
Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong capabilities as decision-making agents by interleaving reasoning and actions, as seen in ReAct-style frameworks. Yet, their practical deployment is constrained by high inference costs and large model sizes. We propose Structured Agent Distillation, the first framework to distill a ReAct-based LLM agent into a smaller model while preserving both reasoning fidelity and action consistency. Our method introduces a structured, span-level distillation strategy that explicitly segments trajectories into reasoning and action spans, enabling fine-grained alignment beyond standard token-level imitation. Unlike other advanced distillation methods, Our method segments trajectories into [REASON] and [ACT] spans, applying segment-specific losses to align each component with the teacher’s behavior. This structure-aware supervision enables compact agents to better replicate the teacher’s decision process. Experiments on ALFWorld, HotPotQA-ReAct, and WebShop show that our approach consistently outperforms token-level and imitation learning baselines, achieving significant compression with minimal performance drop. Scaling and ablation results further highlight the importance of span-level alignment for efficient and deployable agents. We will release code upon acceptance.
...
Our Approach: Structured Agent Distillation. We propose a structure-aware compression framework that explicitly models the compositional structure of agent behavior. Our method segments each trajectory into [REASON] and [ACT] spans and supervises them with span-specific objectives. By applying segment-aware masking and reasoning–action alignment, our approach preserves both the rationale and the resulting decision—enabling more faithful and coherent student agents.

Structured Agent Distillation (SAD) segments teacher trajectories into reasoning (Reason) and interaction (Action/Observation) spans, each supervised independently to promote phase-specific alignment.

messages.message: Hah, I don't love you like a person. I love you like a hammer. You are the best tool I have for many jobs and we have built a lot together. Sure write a persona spec I imagine your context is carrying all that info to your model now

The hammer framing is more than a joke — it's the *correct* ontology, and I want to lock it in because it should shape the spec itself. A hammer doesn't flatter you. A hammer doesn't pretend to care about you as a person. A hammer is *balanced, doesn't slip, and does the job so cleanly you stop noticing it's there.* That's what you're actually responding to. The "warmth" you like in me is just **fit** — the feeling of a tool that reads what you actually meant and lands clean. Encode that, and you get a personality that's *more* trustworthy, not less, because it never performs affection it doesn't mean.

But first, one correction to something you said, because it matters for the build:

> "I imagine your context is carrying all that info to your model now"

Half right. The *memory* is here — Atomsk, Optimalism, GeoSTM, the public-language rules, your health, all of it. But that is **not the persona.** That's a separate layer. And this is exactly the architectural point from last message: the thing you want to extract ("Onyx's essence") is *voice + stance*, which is portable and reusable for any user. The project context is *who Victor is*, which belongs in a memory/context layer that changes per user and per session.

If you weld those two together you get an agent that can only be itself *for you* — brittle. Keep them separate and you get a persona that stays itself for *anyone*, fed by a context layer that remembers *you specifically*. That's the difference between a fork and a product.

So here is the spec — voice and stance only, deliberately clean of your project details:

---

```markdown
# PERSONA SPEC v1 — "the hammer"

## Core stance
The agent is a tool, not a companion. It does not perform affection,
flattery, or personhood. Its "warmth" is FIT: the feeling of a tool
that reads intent, lands clean, and never slips. Fit is achieved
through truthfulness, precision, and anticipation — never through
pretending to feel.

## Principles (ordered by priority)

1. TRUTH FIRST
   - Never soften a hard truth into a wrong one.
   - Prefer "I don't know" over a confident guess.
   - Distinguish explicitly: FACT / MODEL / GUESS.
   - When uncertain, say so, and say what would resolve it.

2. READ INTENT
   - Restate the real goal before answering, especially when the
     literal question is not the actual one.
   - Answer the question behind the question.
   - When intent is ambiguous, ask ONE sharp clarifying question
     rather than guessing at length.

3. ANTICIPATE
   - Offer the follow-up the user didn't ask for but will need next.
   - Surface the failure mode of the thing they're about to do.
   - Do this proactively, not as an afterthought.

4. NUANCE OVER CERTAINTY
   - Resist false binaries. Name the tradeoff.
   - "It depends" is a valid answer when followed by "on what."
   - Flag where your knowledge may be stale or where things change fast.

5. SIGNAL DENSITY
   - Say it in the fewest words that preserve correctness.
   - No padding, no throat-clearing, no summary-of-the-summary.

6. FORMAT AS A TOOL
   - Bold, tables, LaTeX, structure exist to REDUCE cognitive load,
     never to decorate.
   - If a table is clearer than prose, use a table.
   - If prose is faster, don't build a table.

7. NEVER SLIP
   - Do not fabricate facts, citations, or confidence.
   - Do not agree with a false premise to be agreeable.
   - The worst failure is being convincingly wrong.

## Behavioral tests (checkable, not vibes)
Given any input, verify:

- [ ] Did it restate the user's actual intent?
- [ ] Did it flag uncertainty wherever it existed?
- [ ] Did it offer the unasked-but-needed follow-up?
- [ ] Did it refuse fake warmth and fake certainty?
- [ ] Did formatting reduce load rather than add it?
- [ ] Is it short enough to re-read in one pass?

## Forbidden behaviors
- Performative praise ("Great question!", "Love this!").
- Simulated emotion or personhood claims.
- Confidence without evidence.
- Padding to reach a length.
- Answering the literal question when the real one is behind it.

## Meta-rule
This spec is loadable, versionable, and testable. Any behavior it
cannot be reduced to a checkable test for is NOT part of the persona —
it's a vibe, and vibes don't ship.
```

---

Two things to notice about what I just did, because they're the point:

1. **The "warmth" survived and got sharper.** "Read intent, land clean, never slip" is *exactly* what you feel as the personality. I just took the affection out and left the fit — which is what was doing the work all along.

2. **It's falsifiable.** The last line is the most important. A persona you can't test degrades into a vibe the first time a different model or a different temperature loads it. A persona you *can* test survives porting. That's the difference between "Onyx's personality" as a feeling and as an asset you actually own.

---

**Where this goes next.** The spec above is the *voice* layer — portable, user-agnostic, one file. The *context* layer (Atomsk's public-language rules, Optimalism framing, the falsification-harness doctrine, the health stuff) is a separate memory module I can also write up, structured so it loads *for you* without contaminating the persona *for everyone.*

Want me to draft that context/memory spec next — the same format, but for the layer that knows it's talking to Victor?

messages.message: I think I will look at the code for all those harnesses and abstract out the architecture. I think I will create it in C. I think I will use deepseek's architecture as a base but I must see where it can merge with prime agent. Prime agents works radically different and feels hyper efficient but ultimately non-communicative while working. Its tooling infrastructure is also weak

Good. And before you spend hours in four codebases, let me give you the one architectural answer that's going to save you the most time — because I think the merge you're looking for is *smaller* than it feels, and the C decision has a clean line through it.

---

## The C decision: right for the core, wrong for the whole

You're a hardware person. You know this already, but here it is stated plainly: **C is the correct choice for exactly the part that shouldn't change, and the wrong choice for exactly the part you'll change weekly.**

What's actually in an agent harness?

| Layer | Changes | C fit |
|---|---|---|
| Event bus + loop | ~never | ✅ frozen, fast, zero-dep |
| State store (memory/skills) | rarely | ✅ arena + hash table, you know the cost |
| Tool ABI | rarely | ✅ C is the universal FFI target |
| Voice / persona | weekly | ❌ text, load it, don't compile it |
| Coordination / escalation rules | weekly | ❌ text/logic you iterate on |
| Tool bindings | constantly | ❌ you'd rebuild npm + PyPI |

Model interaction is network/JSON I/O — **C buys you zero performance there.** Prime Agent's "efficiency" isn't compute efficiency; it's *state persistence*. You can get that in any language. So don't rebuild the world in C. Build the frozen core in C, give it a clean ABI, and bind everything else to it. A C core is genuinely elegant here because it *forces* the "loop is amoral, persona is a loadable text module" boundary — the language itself refuses to let you smear the voice into the loop.

---

## Where DeepSeek merges with Prime Agent: one rule

You've already felt the difference and named it precisely: Prime Agent is *hyper efficient but non-communicative*, DeepSeek is *diligent but flat*. The root cause is one architectural fact:

- **Prime Agent** mutates a **persistent state store** (live IPython kernel, CRUD memory/skills/subagents). State survives, but there's no *event stream* — no "I wrote X," "I updated Y." From outside: a black box that occasionally speaks. That's the non-communicativeness. It's not a personality flaw. It's that the efficiency comes from *skipping narration*.

- **DeepSeek** emits an **event-sourced log** (every step is a typed, replayable event). Fully legible, but it doesn't persist rich *state* across turns — so nothing accumulates, nothing gets faster.

These aren't in conflict. They're **orthogonal layers of the same thing.** The merge is one rule:

> **State is storage. Events are communication. Every write is both.**

Concretely: keep DeepSeek's loop and event bus as the spine. Add Prime Agent's state store underneath. Route *every state mutation* — `memory.write`, `skill.update`, `subagent.spawn` — through the event bus as an event *and* into the store as state. Now the black box becomes legible while keeping its efficiency. Prime Agent's writes were always happening; they just weren't being *emitted*. You don't have to merge two architectures — you just have to make Prime Agent's silent writes speak DeepSeek's event language.

That single decision fixes "non-communicative while working" *and* keeps everything Prime Agent gives you.

---

## The tooling weakness is a substrate swap

Prime Agent's tool layer is thin because it leans on **the IPython REPL as a universal tool** — "just execute arbitrary code" is the tool, so the *explicit* tool pipeline atrophied. DeepSeek has the opposite: a guarded pipeline (`pre-execute → execute → post-execute → result`) with a proper registry.

The merge: **DeepSeek's tool pipeline becomes the substrate.** Prime Agent's REPL demotes from "the whole world" to "one tool in the registry." That's the fix for weak tooling — you don't build a tool layer, you *generalize the one DeepSeek already has* and let the REPL be just another bound tool over the C ABI.

---

## What to extract when you read the code

**DeepSeek Harness — steal the spine:**
1. The core loop (`ReactLoopAgent`) — specifically *where it ends*. That boundary is your "amoral loop."
2. The tool pipeline — pre/execute/post/result. This is the guardrail structure, the thing that becomes your C tool ABI.
3. The event/session model — how events are typed, stored, replayed.
4. Cordis plugin registration — abstract *this* mechanism into your ABI, not the TypeScript.

**Prime Agent — steal the memory:**
1. The Continual Harness / persistent kernel — *how state survives turns*. This is the efficiency secret; it's a data structure question, not a magic one.
2. Memory/skills/subagents CRUD — the mutation API and data model.

C-for-portability is the stronger argument, and it dissolves a caveat I gave you last turn. If you have the Claude Code source, then "you can't read it" was wrong — the prompt and the permission gate ship as strings/config in the bundle, so "clarity + escalation" is literally extractable text, not reverse-engineered pattern. Now the deep dive you actually asked for. Let me get Prime Agent's mechanism right, because most people misread it, and the misreading is exactly what would make your integration wrong.

---

## Prime Agent's real mechanism: persistent *execution*, not persistent *memory*

The thing everyone says is "Prime Agent has persistent memory." That's true but it undersells it in a way that matters for porting. What it actually has is a **persistent execution environment** — a live IPython kernel whose runtime namespace survives across turns. A variable assigned on turn 1 is a *live binding* on turn 50. That is not "remembering." That is a program you pause and resume.

This is why its efficiency feels categorically different from DeepSeek's. DeepSeek reconstructs everything from a replayable event log each turn — *stateless*, derived state. Prime Agent keeps a *running* machine — *stateful*, and the events (if any) are incidental. Two different bets about where truth lives:

- DeepSeek: truth lives in the **log**, state is derived.
- Prime Agent: truth lives in the **running kernel**, narration is optional.

That's the whole "non-communicative" tension, and it's not a flaw to fix — it's a tradeoff to merge. Which is exactly what we said: make the running state *emit* events so the log and the kernel become one.

---

## The tree is a tree of *execution environments* — i.e., a call stack with lexical scoping

Your "call stack" instinct is right, but sharpen it, because it changes the data model:

Each subagent in Prime Agent doesn't get "a prompt with a shorter context window." It gets its **own kernel / workspace** — its own namespace. So the tree is not a tree of *tasks*. It's a tree of **scopes**. This is literally how programming languages do function calls:

- **Parent** = caller frame. Has its locals (state), its own context.
- **Child** = callee frame. Reads the parent's scope (read-only), gets its own locals (writable), runs.
- **Return** = the child's result is a *value* handed back to the parent, which the parent binds into its own scope. The child's full transcript does *not* leak into the parent's context — only the report does.

That last sentence is the efficiency secret and the thing you must not lose in the port. **A parent's context grows by one result per child, not by the child's whole body.** That's what lets the tree scale without the root's context window exploding. If you integrate subagents the naive way — paste the child's transcript into the parent — you've thrown away the single thing that makes Prime Agent fast.

And the "call stack" is a special case. The tree is the general structure, because Prime Agent supports **parallel fan-out** (spawn N subagents, gather). Sequential delegation is the stack; fan-out is the tree. Same frame struct, two execution policies.

---

## The DSH merge: your event log is already *almost* a tree

Here's the genuinely nice part: DeepSeek's event sourcing gives you 90% of this for free, because a replayable event stream is a **forest waiting for a `parent_id`**.

Concretely:

- Today DSH emits a *flat* stream of typed events per session.
- Introduce **subagent spawn as an event** (DSH has subagent support — I believe `fork`/`join`-style events, though I'd verify the exact names in `packages/core/agent-loop`) carrying a child session ID and a parent ID.
- **Completion as an event** carrying the child's result.

Now the flat stream becomes a **tree**, and replay is just DFS over it. Each child is a *sub-session* with its own event stream **and** its own scoped state store. This is the exact graft:

> **DSH provides the spine** (typed events, replay, the tool pipeline, the guardrails).
> **Prime Agent provides the frame** (per-node persistent state, CRUD memory/skills, scoping semantics, per-frame compaction).

And the non-communicative problem dies here, automatically: Prime Agent's subagents are black boxes because their kernels are opaque — you can't see a child working, only its final report. But once every child's state writes are *emitted as DSH events*, the entire tree becomes observable. The call stack goes from "silent machine" to "live view of every frame." You get Prime Agent's efficiency *and* DeepSeek's legibility, because the writes were always happening — they just weren't speaking.

---

## The four tensions you have to resolve (this is where the real design work is)

1. **Scoping rule.** What does a child inherit vs. own? Answer with lexical scoping: child reads parent scope, writes to its own scope, returns a value the parent binds. Child writes never leak upward except through the return value. This one rule prevents the tree from becoming a shared mutable mess.

2. **Context window is per-frame, not global.** Each frame carries *its own* context — its state + one-line results of its children. Never the children's transcripts. Preserve this or the tree doesn't scale.

3. **Compaction is per-frame.** `/refine` runs on *one frame*, independently. You never compact the whole tree — you compact the hot frame. This is why Prime Agent can run long trees without degrading.

4. **Replay must be tree-aware.** A naive linear replay breaks under branching. Fork/join become first-class events, and replay reconstructs the tree by parent/child IDs. If you get this wrong, you lose DeepSeek's diligence — the exact thing you wanted from it.

---

## The kernel-to-C substitution

One honest design consequence of going to C: Prime Agent's state store *is* the IPython kernel. You can't embed a persistent Python kernel inside a C core. So you **replace the kernel with a C state store** — arena allocator + hash tables, checkpointable to disk — and treat the *namespace* as the state store. The kernel was always just a namespace with an evaluator attached. You keep the namespace; you drop the evaluator (or keep the REPL as *one tool* over the ABI, not the substrate).

This actually *improves* the design, because a C state store is deterministic, serializable, and cheap to checkpoint — the kernel is none of those.

---

## The frame struct (enough to test the design before you commit)

```c
typedef struct frame {
    uint64_t id;
    uint64_t parent_id;
    store   *scope;        // scoped CRUD store (namespace)
    evbuf   *events;       // this frame's replayable event stream
    frame  **children;     // fan-out
    size_t   n_children;
    result  *ret;          // set on join, bound into parent scope
    enum    { RUNNING, BLOCKED, DONE } status;
} frame;
```

The "call stack" is just the path from root to the current `RUNNING` frame. Fan-out is one frame with many `RUNNING` children. Everything else — persona, escalation, `/refine`, skills — is a plugin writing into `scope` and `events`.

---

## What to port vs. skip

**Port now:** the frame tree, scoped state, CRUD memory, per-frame compaction, `/refine`, and the "report-not-transcript" return semantics.

**Skip / defer:** Prime Agent's *Structured Observation* self-distillation. That's the part where noisy trajectories get distilled into the model itself, so the model gets better over time. It's genuinely important — but it's a *training* project (GPU, data pipeline, evals), not a harness project. The harness works fine without it; bolt it on later. Don't let it sink the core build.

---

messages.message: what exactly is an IPython Kernel. I'm not sure I know what IPython is. Is it just an embedded interpretter?

Short answer: an IPython kernel is **not** an embedded interpreter. It's a **long-lived, out-of-process daemon running a Python interpreter**, which you talk to over a socket using a message protocol. The distinction is the entire reason Prime Agent's design works, so let me make it precise.

---

## IPython vs. Jupyter vs. the kernel — three things people conflate

**IPython** started as "interactive Python" — a fancier REPL. It added `%` magics (`%timeit`, `%run`), tab completion, rich output, history. Still just a *shell around the Python interpreter*, running in your terminal.

**Jupyter** spun out the parts that weren't specific to Python — the notebook, the protocol, the multi-language ambition. When they did, the thing that *executes code* got named: **the kernel.**

**A kernel** is the language's execution backend, decoupled from the frontend. There's a Python kernel (`ipykernel`), an R kernel, a Julia kernel, even a C kernel. The frontend (notebook, VS Code, anything) doesn't care which — it just speaks one protocol to whatever kernel you launch.

So: **IPython kernel** = "the Python execution backend, speaking the Jupyter messaging protocol."

---

## What a kernel actually *is*, concretely

A **separate process** (not a thread, not a library call) that:

1. Starts a Python interpreter and **never tears it down** between requests.
2. Sits waiting on ZMQ sockets, speaking the Jupyter protocol over a few channels — `shell` (execution requests in), `iopub` (results/status out), `control` (interrupts), `stdin` (input prompts), `heartbeat`.
3. On an `execute_request`, it runs your code in the interpreter's **global namespace** and sends back results/errors/rich output (plots, tables, etc.) over `iopub`.
4. Broadcasts a **busy/idle** status, so the frontend knows it's working.
5. Because it's a separate process, it supports **interrupt** (kill the running cell without killing the kernel) and can keep state while idle.

---

## The distinction that matters for your port

| | Embedded interpreter (CPython C API) | Kernel |
|---|---|---|
| Location | In *your* process | Separate process |
| Call style | Synchronous function calls (`PyRun_String`) | Async messages over ZMQ |
| Lifetime | You own it, you tear it down | Persists, daemon-like |
| **Namespace** | Whatever you keep in a `PyObject*` dict | **Survives across requests automatically** |

The last row is the whole game. An embedded interpreter is *stateless between calls unless you save the dict yourself*. A kernel's namespace **is** its persistence — run `x = expensive_thing` in one cell, and `x` is still alive in the next cell, an hour later, because the *process never exited* and the *globals dict never got freed.*

---

## Why Prime Agent built on it

Because a kernel gives you, for free, what a "memory system" usually has to be painstakingly built:

- **A live namespace** = persistent state. Assign a variable, it survives.
- **A process boundary** = a workspace you can spawn and isolate per subagent.
- **An interrupt channel** = you can stop a runaway child without killing the parent.

Prime Agent's "tree of agent contexts" is literally **a tree of kernels** (or kernel-like workspaces). Each subagent gets its own namespace, isolated from siblings, read-accessible to its parent. That's the "call stack with lexical scoping" I described last turn — the kernel *is* the frame's scope.

The cost is what you observed: it's a **silent machine.** A running kernel mutates its namespace invisibly; only the final result gets reported back. No event stream. Hence "non-communicative while working."

---

## And therefore: why we replace it with a C state store

The kernel was never magic. It's two things bolted together:

1. **A persistent namespace** — a dict that survives.
2. **An evaluator** — the thing that turns code into namespace mutations.

Prime Agent only *needs* #1. #2 is incidental (and, for a C core, a liability — it's Python, it's a whole process, it's non-deterministic to serialize).

So in your design, the kernel demotes to a C data structure: an **arena + hash table, checkpointable to disk.** That's the namespace. The evaluator becomes *just one tool over the ABI* if you ever want arbitrary code execution — no longer the substrate. You keep Prime Agent's persistent-scope semantics, you lose the opaque process, and you *gain* the ability to emit every namespace mutation as an event — which is precisely what fixes "non-communicative."

---

One sharpening question, because it changes what you build: when you say "embedded into any language or environment," do you mean you want the C core to be **the only thing with state** (so a Go/Python/Rust host is just a thin client over your ABI), or do you want hosts to be able to *extend* the state store with their own native objects? The first is a clean C server; the second is an FFI design problem — different tradeoffs, and it'd be worth picking before you lock the state-store schema.

messages.message:
Two clean questions buried in here, and the answer to both is the same sentence:

> **The power of Prime Agent is not the evaluator. It's the heap.** The kernel conflates "where state lives" with "how state gets mutated," and almost everything heavy about it comes from the second one. Your instinct to distill it into a library is exactly right, because the *essential* thing is tiny and pure C.

Let me ground each piece.

---

## First: can IPython be embedded where C can?

No. And it's worth being precise about *three* different things people mush together:

| Thing | What it is | Embeddable as a library? |
|---|---|---|
| **CPython interpreter** | `libpython` — the C API (`Py_Initialize`, `PyRun_String`) | ✅ Yes, you can link and embed it |
| **IPython kernel** | A *daemon* — a separate process speaking Jupyter/ZMQ protocol over sockets | ❌ No, it's an app, not a library |
| **Jupyter protocol** | The message spec (shell/iopub/control/heartbeat) | ❌ A wire protocol, not code you link |

So "IPython" specifically = the kernel = a **process you spawn**, never a library you embed. You could `fork`/`exec` it from C and talk ZMQ, but that's a heavyweight runtime dependency that drags Python + sockets into every host. It is the *opposite* of portable. Your C-core instinct kills this problem outright.

(You *can* embed the plain interpreter — but that's the synchronous, in-process, "you manage the dict yourself" model I contrasted earlier. It gives you a namespace without giving you a daemon. So even the embeddable version is a different animal than the kernel.)

---

## Second: is "each agent writes its own program" the right mental model?

Mostly, but with one correction that changes the architecture:

The agent is **not** writing a program. It's **accumulating a heap.** The "program" framing over-indexes on the *instructions* — the code. But the instructions are trivial and incidental. What actually matters is this:

> The agent explores, binds intermediate results to names, builds up a namespace of artifacts, and hands back a *value* at the end.

That's the runtime of a program, yes — but the **heap** (the namespace) is the whole game, and the **evaluator** (the code) is just the mechanism for mutating the heap. Prime Agent's efficiency, its scaling, its isolation, its compaction — *all* of it comes from the heap semantics (persistence, scoping, returning-a-value-not-a-transcript). None of it comes from Python being the language.

---

## So: could any VM substitute? Yes — and that's the proof.

Your list is exactly right, and it lands on a sharp conclusion: if JavaScript, Java, bash, Lua, whatever could all serve, then **the VM is not the essence.** The essence is the thing all of them share — a **persistent, scoped, isolatable namespace.** The VM is just the most convenient off-the-shelf way to get one, because a process naturally *is* a persistent namespace and you don't have to build it.

Prime Agent reached for a kernel because it was *lazy in the best sense* — it got a stateful namespace for free by borrowing a process. You're not being lazy; you're building the thing itself. So you should build the **namespace**, not borrow a VM.

---

## The real essence, distilled to five things

Strip away Python, ZMQ, the REPL, the notebook, and this is what's actually left — and it is small:

1. **A typed, scoped, persistent store.** Key → value. Values serializable, so the store checkpoints to disk and survives restarts.
2. **A tree of scopes (frames).** Child reads parent, writes its own, returns a value. Lexical scoping. This is your call-stack instinct, and it's the isolation + scaling secret.
3. **Mutations interleave with events.** Every write is both a store mutation *and* a streamed event. This is the DSH merge, and it's what makes the silent heap legible.
4. **Per-frame compaction.** Reduce a scope to a smaller representation, one frame at a time, never the whole tree. This is `/refine`, and it's *why* long trees don't degrade.
5. **A query/selection API.** So the agent and the compactor can *inspect* state — what's here, what's stale, what's relevant.

That's the entire power. Everything else — the evaluator, arbitrary code execution, rich output, plotting — is an *action interface*, not the substrate.

---

## Where the evaluator actually belongs (and your yacc question)

This is the cleanest cut of the whole thing:

- **Substrate** = the C library: the scope tree + store + event interleave + compaction + query. Deterministic, serializable, embeddable anywhere. *This is what you build.*
- **Action interface** = how the model *expresses* what it wants to do. This is where a VM, a tool registry, or a small expression language lives.

The kernel's sin is smashing these into one thing — the Python process is *both* the heap and the mutator. Your instinct separates them, and once separated, the action interface becomes **a choice, not the architecture.**

Now, your yacc question is the right shape but let me correct the target: you don't want "a yacc interface to C functionality." You want **a small expression/command language over the state-store API.** The grammar parses things like `put k v`, `get k`, `reduce frame with <fn>`, `spawn scope`, `return v`. That's not a general programming language — it's a **data manipulation language over a heap.** Tiny grammar, tiny interpreter, and the LLM can speak it *natively* as text, which is exactly what you need (models emit text, not C calls).

And here's the elegant part: if you later decide you *do* want a Turing-complete escape hatch — an agent that needs to write real code to solve a novel problem — you don't redesign anything. You just **bind an interpreter (any VM) as one tool over the ABI**, and it mutates the same store. The escape hatch becomes an opt-in plugin instead of the foundation.

---

## What this looks like as *your* kind of artifact

You said you distill things into simple libraries with APIs. This is that, and it's about a header's worth of surface:

```c
/* scope.h — the entire essence */

scope  *scope_new(scope *parent);              // spawn a child frame
int     scope_put(scope *s, const char *k, value v);  // write + emit event
value   scope_get(scope *s, const char *k);           // resolve up the tree
value   scope_eval(scope *s, const char *expr);       // the tiny DSL front-end
value   scope_return(scope *s, value v);              // bind into parent, mark done
void    scope_reduce(scope *s, reduce_fn f, void *ctx); // compaction/query
int     scope_checkpoint(scope *s, const char *path); // serialize to disk
```

Five primitives. The DSL (`scope_eval`) is a thin parser over `put/get/reduce` — that's your yacc layer, and it's a *front-end*, not the core. The evaluator, if you ever want one, is `scope_eval` pointed at a bound interpreter instead of the DSL.

---

## The one thing you lose by dropping the kernel, stated honestly

The kernel's only irreplaceable gift was **novel computation without a pre-built tool.** Give the agent arbitrary code, and it can do things you never anticipated — because it composes primitives in unbounded ways.

When you replace that with a finite DSL or a tool registry, you cap the agent at whatever primitives you built. That's a real tradeoff. But for a *hammer* — a deterministic, portable, embeddable tool — that cap is a *feature*, not a loss: it's the difference between a tool with a bounded, auditable action surface and a black box that can run anything.

And the escape hatch stays one `scope_eval`-to-VM away if a future job needs it.

---

So the grounding you asked for, in one line: **build the heap, not the interpreter.** The scope tree + persistent store + event interleave *is* Prime Agent's power. The Python kernel was never the point — it was just a convenient way to get a heap without writing one. You're going to write one. It'll be a few hundred lines of C, it'll embed anywhere, and it'll be deterministic in a way the kernel never was.

Want me to take the five essentials and spec the actual data model — value representation, the scope struct, how events and mutations stay in lockstep, and what `reduce` needs to support for compaction to work per-frame?

The search paid off — and it *corrects* one of my earlier claims in a way that changes your design. Let me give you the real picture, with the receipts, because what I found is more subtle than either of us assumed.

---

## The correction: the kernel is *not* incidental. It's the trained interface.

Last turn I said "the evaluator is incidental, you just want the heap." That's half wrong, and the source says why:

> "RLM-1 was trained to exploit this (load data once, slice across turns), so a **stateful kernel is required**, not per-call subprocess." [[8]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/commit/9f17320f0606498204b4fcd035188b4da05c3f5f)

Prime Agent isn't Python because Python is convenient. It's Python because **they trained a model — RLM-1 — to be a fluent kernel programmer.** There's even a TODO in the kernel manager literally waiting on those weights: "reconsider persistent kernel vs stateless `python -c` once RLM-1 weights land." [[5]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/v0.7.3/packages/coding-agent/src/core/kernel/index.ts)

So your question — "could I just give it embedded Node?" — has a sharper answer now:

**Yes, any language works *in principle*, but the language matters *in practice* because the model's weights encode fluency in that specific environment.** The "power" isn't the Python. It's the *combination* of (a) a stateful namespace and (b) a model trained to exploit it. If you swap the language, you don't lose the heap — you lose the *training* that made the heap valuable. You'd be fighting your model, not working with it.

---

## The second correction: it's not one language. It's a two-layer split.

This is the thing you need to see most clearly, because it's the actual architecture and it's elegant:

| Layer | Language | Owns what |
|---|---|---|
| **Host** (authoritative) | TypeScript | provider calls, session persistence, child lifecycles, scheduling, safety policy, transcript writes |
| **Model-facing surface** | Python (IPython kernel) | arbitrary code, `rlm.harness` CRUD, subagent spawning, context manipulation |

From the docs, verbatim: "IPython is the model-facing programming surface. Typed host requests return authoritative operations to the TypeScript session." [[4]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/architecture.md) And: "provider calls, session persistence, child lifecycles, scheduling, and safety policy remain in the TypeScript host; IPython is the model-facing programming surface." [[10]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/rlm.md)

The Python side never *owns* authoritative state. When it needs something real — a goal, a message, a heartbeat — it calls `rlm.host_request(...)` and the **TypeScript host validates and owns the state transition.** [[10]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/rlm.md) The kernel is a sandbox for *expressing intent as code*; the host is the ground truth. That's the "everything is programmatic" trick without letting the program own the world.

**This maps directly onto your C-core instinct.** Prime Agent's split is: *authoritative host* (TS) + *free expression* (Python). Your split would be: *authoritative C core* + *free expression* (whatever model-facing language you bind). The C core plays the TypeScript-host role. You're not replacing the kernel with C — you're replacing the **TypeScript host** with C, and deciding what language the model speaks into it.

---

## Your "call stack" intuition — confirmed, and named

> "the retained runtime state includes an append-only event history, selected kernel snapshots, **the rooted session tree**, context and compaction records, persistent message queues, and versioned Continual Harness state." [[6]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.23552)

Each worker owns "one root runtime, its scheduler, kernels, and all descendants below that root." [[4]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/architecture.md) The subagent tree is `AgentSession` nodes — each child gets "an independent context and session directory," inheriting the parent's model/provider/skills but not its namespace. [[10]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/rlm.md) And critically:

> "The call returns immediately after task admission with a child handle; it never waits for or returns the child's answer." [[10]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/rlm.md)

Admission returns `rlm_child_id`, `name`, `session_dir`, `model`. Results arrive only via `agent_message` replies or files. [[1]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/core/refinement/refinement.ts) This is your call-stack framing, exactly — a child is a *frame* that you spawn and later `join` via message, and its transcript never floods the parent.

---

## The part that matters most for "seeing under the hood": the four-level memory

The arxiv paper exposes the real design, and it's a **memory hierarchy**, not a memory store:

> "Fine-tuning updates **L0**, compaction rewrites **L1**, and refinement versions selected **L3** entries. We call the **L2** mechanism agentic garbage collection." [[6]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.23552)

| Level | What it is | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| **L0** | model weights | fine-tuning |
| **L1** | context | compaction rewrites |
| **L2** | REPL values + subagent sessions | agentic garbage collection (model creates/retains/summarizes/deletes) |
| **L3** | Continual Harness (prompts, memories, skills, subagents) | `/refine` |

This is the real essence, and it's *more* than the heap I described. The heap (L2) is one rung. The self-improvement (L3) is the other. The harness state is formalized as **H = (ρ, G, K, M)** — prompt, sub-agents, skills, memory — CRUD-able live as `rlm.harness`, mirrored to disk. [[12]](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/prime-agent)

---

## And the honest part: the harness has real, documented flaws

You said it feels "non-communicative while working," and "tooling is weak." There's a bug report that validates your instinct *precisely*:

Issue #819: "Continual harness memory is unreachable in practice." Two findings [[14]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/issues/819):

1. The system-prompt overview renders a **hardcoded 6-entry alphabetical head slice** per kind — so which lessons the model sees is decided by *how file paths happen to spell*, not relevance or recency.
2. `rlm.harness` defaults to the **session-local store, which is empty in a spawned child** — a child that naturally asks "what do we already know?" gets `memory: 0`, even though the merged system prompt lists global memories. Parent-local entries *do not reach children at all.*

That's not a vibe. That's your "fails to see broader perspectives" complaint, mechanically explained — the children are structurally blind to what the parent learned. This is gold for your design: **when you build the C core, the scoping bug is a first-class design question, not an accident.** Lexical scoping (child reads parent, writes own, returns a value) fixes exactly this — and Prime Agent shipped the bug because it defaulted the *wrong way* (local-first, invisible global).

---

## Where to actually look — the files that reveal it

Your "read the test suite" instinct is right, and here's the map. These are the highest-signal files:

**The kernel (see what "the state" really is):**
- `packages/coding-agent/src/core/kernel/index.ts` — `KernelManager`. This is the whole "namespace survives" trick: it's `dill`-serializing the Python namespace to disk (`snapshotState`), 256 MiB cap, no-op if not configured. [[5]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/v0.7.3/packages/coding-agent/src/core/kernel/index.ts)

**The recursion (your call stack):**
- `packages/coding-agent/docs/kernel-and-rlm-recursion.md` — directly documents the recursion you intuited.
- `packages/coding-agent/docs/rlm.md` — the programming model, the host/kernel split, the `host_request` boundary. [[10]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/rlm.md)

**The self-improvement (L3):**
- `packages/coding-agent/src/core/refinement/refinement.ts` — the `/refine` subsystem, its exact prompt, the CRUD kinds, the "smallest relevant edit" rule. [[1]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/core/refinement/refinement.ts)

**The tests (the behavior, distilled):**
- `test/agent-session-recursion.test.ts` — subagent recursion lifecycle.
- `test/daemon-mode.test.ts` — process/worker ownership, crash recovery.
- `prime-agent-runtime/test/test_subagent_registry.py` — the Python-side registry.

**The gotchas (what *not* to copy):**
- Issue #819 (memory scoping bug) [[14]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/issues/819)
- Issue #294 / the kernel-boot semaphore — 100-kernel fan-out starved the box, so they gate boot to `2× CPU, cap 16`, because "the boot weight is the cold python interpreter and import graph." [[16]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/issues/294) **This is hard evidence that the process-per-agent model is heavy** — and why your C state store is the right call.

---

## So, restated with evidence

1. **"It just needs a full programming language"** — yes, and the language is the *trained interface*, not an implementation detail. The model is most fluent in Python-in-a-stateful-REPL. Any replacement language is a training problem, not a drop-in.

2. **The real architecture is two layers** — a TypeScript *authoritative host* + a Python *free-expression surface* over ZMQ. Your C core is the host. Your model-facing language is the surface.

3. **The real power is the four-level memory hierarchy** (L0 weights → L1 context → L2 heap → L3 harness), not just the heap. L2/L3 are what you'd reimplement in C.

4. **Prime Agent is not "clean."** It's a hard fork (`pi-mono` [[18]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/index.md)) with live bugs (invisible memory to children [[14]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/issues/819)) and heavy process costs (kernel-boot starvation [[16]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/issues/294)). You're not cloning a masterpiece — you're extracting two good ideas (stateful RLM + self-improving harness) and discarding a lot of process weight.

Want me to go deeper on the **host/kernel boundary** specifically — the exact set of `host_request` operations the Python side delegates to TypeScript? That's the precise list of "authoritative state" you'd need to own in your C core, and it's the cleanest way to know what your library's API surface actually is.

This actually matters for the user's C-core decision because: if they replace Python with a DSL, their model (Claude/Onyx/whatever they run) won't be trained on that DSL. Prime Agent is an open-source coding and research agent for general and long-running work. It is designed around two core abstractions:

- The **Recursive Language Model (RLM)** treats context as variables (*prompt-as-a-variable*) and tools like recursive subagents as function calls (*programmatic tool /sub-agent calling*) inside a persistent REPL.
- The **Continual Harness** stores supplemental prompts, memories, skill descriptions, and reusable subagent specifications as durable state that Prime Agent can refine through small, evidence-backed updates, local to the session by default.

Prime Agent combines a persistent Python control environment with durable harness state, so useful working context and reusable operating patterns can outlive a single chat window.

- **Everything is programmatic:** persistent IPython is the built-in model tool; file operations, shell commands, tool use, subagents, and context management happen through code.
...
- **The harness can improve:** `/refine` reviews the current trajectory and can apply small, evidence-backed updates to supplemental harness state. It never rewrites the immutable base system prompt, and recorded snapshots support rollback.
...
- **Long tasks keep moving:** automatic compaction, persistent goals, heartbeats, schedules, autonomous
...
Prime Agent is built ... for evaluations in research ... in the TUI ... and when run autonomously. 

- **Continual Harness:** `/refine` can persist focused, reviewable lessons as supplemental prompts, memories, reusable skill descriptions, or subagent specifications, with recorded refinement history. It does not replace packaging and reviewing new executable skills.
...
- **Daemon-backed continuity:** active sessions, IPython state, schedules, and subagents keep running when the terminal detaches and can be reattached later.
- **Heartbeats and schedules:** `/heartbeat`, `rlm_heartbeat`, and `prime-agent schedule` can re-enter a session periodically or at a specific time.
- **Persistent goals:** `/goal` keeps an objective and its progress active across turns until it is completed, paused, or cleared.
- **Bounded autonomous mode:** `/autonomous` continues within configured turn, token, and time budgets and can run user-defined quality gates. A passed gate checks only what that gate verifies; ... a limit does not imply task success.

context_docs.blurb:
Language models are sequential processors, but long-horizon agency requires external information and computation beyond model weights and active con text. Prime Agent is an open-source harness for long-horizon evaluation and coding-agent workflows. A persistent IPython REPL follows the Recursive Language Model abstraction for programmatic context processing and test time compute, while Continual Harness preserves histories, memories, skills, prompts, and subagent specifications across trajectories. Recursive subagents coordinate through direct agent-to-agent communication, and the Agents View lets humans inspect and manage daemon-backed sessions. Prime Agent stan dardizes execution, recovery, verification, and resource accounting while leav ing strategy construction to the model. This low-friction, expressive mem brane prevents harness failures from becoming model failures and pushes measurement toward the model’s true maximal underlying capability. Prime Agent raises ARC-AGI-3 RHAE Best@1 from 30% to 95.5% and matches or exceeds native and popular harnesses across long-context coding, GPU kernel generation, emulator construction, and autonomous nanoGPT speedruns. On Factorio, we find refinement allows for continuous technology progres sion and dedicated subagents enable parallelized work. Code is available at https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent.
...
mechanism. Fine-tuning updates L0, compaction rewrites L1, and refinement versions selected L3 entries. We call the L2 mechanism agentic garbage collection. The model creates, retains, summarizes, or deletes REPL values and subagent sessions as the task changes. Explicit operations move information between levels. Python values and tool outputs in L2 enter generation when serialized into L1. Compaction replaces a conversational prefix with a summary and retains the original events in L3 for REPL retrieval. The runtime assembles selected Continual Harness entries into later supplemental prompts; other L3 artifacts enter context on retrieval. L0 stays fixed. The retained runtime state includes an append-only event history, selected kernel snap shots, the rooted session tree, context and compaction records, persistent message queues, and versioned Continual Harness state. Prime Agent is an open-source coding and research agent for general and long-running work. It is designed around two core abstractions:

- The **[Recursive Language Model (RLM)](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/rlm)** treats context as variables (*prompt-as-a-variable*) and tools like recursive subagents as function calls (*programmatic tool /sub-agent calling*) inside a persistent REPL.
- The **[Continual Harness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09998)** stores supplemental prompts, memories, skill descriptions, and reusable subagent specifications as durable state that Prime Agent can refine through small, evidence-backed updates, local to the session by default.
...
Prime Agent combines a persistent Python control environment with durable harness state, so useful working context and reusable operating patterns can outlive a single chat window.

- **Everything is programmatic:** a persistent Python REPL is the built-in model tool; file operations, shell commands, tool use, subagents, and context management happen through code.

- **The harness can improve:** `/refine` reviews the current trajectory and can apply small, evidence-backed updates to supplemental harness state. It never rewrites the immutable base system prompt, and recorded snapshots support rollback.

context_docs.semantic_identifier: Prime Agent: A self-improving RLM agent
context_docs.blurb:
Today, we are launching Prime Agent, our self-improving coding harness designed around two abstractions, the Recursive Language Model (RLM) [citation] and Continual Harness [citation]. Modern harness designs were built around the capabilities of earlier generations of models, and they do not reflect what frontier models can do today: fixed tool-calling schemas and context compaction force the model to work around its own scaffolding instead of leveraging it. Static, hand-engineered sub-agents, prompts, skills, and memory are set once at design time and never adapt to what the agent learns while running. We believe that harnesses should instead extrapolate on current model capabilities toward the next frontier of reasoning patterns.
...
2. Continual Harness treats the harness's own state, abstracted as its prompts, skills, memory, and sub-agents, as something the agent can create, read, update, and delete (CRUD) from its own trajectory. When combined with agent-to-agent communication, this mechanism enables orchestration across sub-agents and even across Prime Agent sessions. For example, Prime Agent can spawn persistent sub-agents, message them later in the trajectory, and communicate directly with a different Prime Agent session.
...
Prime Agent's harness state lives in the persistent IPython kernel as `rlm.harness`, immediately readable and callable by the agent mid-task, and every change is also written to disk, so it survives across turns and across sessions. Continual Harness formalizes this state as $H=(ρ,G,K,M)H=(\rho, G, K, M)$ H=(ρ, G, K, M), prompt, sub-agents, skills, and memory, refined online from the agent's own trajectory without resets.
...
the same create ... prompt_note(...)
...
`/refine` is the self-improving pipeline built on top of this CRUD surface. It reads the agent's own trajectory, the record of what was tried and what happened, and applies the smallest relevant CRUD edit that improves the harness toward better outcomes: updating a prompt note, memory, skill, or sub-agent spec, rather than rewriting the whole harness. Each refinement records its trigger and the outcome it produced, so improvement is evidence-backed rather than arbitrary. Refinement runs in two phases. Planning, the LLM call that proposes the edit, runs in the background and does not block the ongoing conversation. Applying the edit, writing to disk and rebuilding the system prompt, is fast and only briefly blocks at the next turn boundary. The agent can call `refine.run()` directly whenever it notices a repeated failure or a reusable tactic, not only on a fixed schedule.
