context_docs.semantic_identifier: Continual harness memory is unreachable in practice: the prompt overview is a hardcoded 6-entry alphabetical head slice, and `rlm.harness` defaults to the session-local store, which is empty in a spawned child
context_docs.blurb:
**A. The system-prompt overview renders an alphabetical head slice of 6 entries per kind at a hardcoded cap.** `formatHarnessStateForPrompt()` renders the continual harness overview into the system prompt using a default cap of 6 entries per kind and a 180-character body clip. The 6 that survive are chosen by an alphabetical sort on `[path, title, id]` — not recency, version, or relevance — so which lessons the model sees is decided by how their file paths happen to be spelled. The function's options object already accepts `maxEntriesPerKind`/`maxContentLength`, but neither production call site passes them, and grepping the published sources turns up no setting, env var, or config key that reaches them — so in practice the limits behave as hardcoded. (If there is a supported way to raise them that we missed, that would resolve most of A.)

**B. `rlm.harness` resolves to the session-local store, which is empty for a spawned child.** `rlm.harness` resolves to the **session-local** harness store by default, and for an `rlm()`-spawned child that store is new and empty at spawn. A child that does the natural thing — `rlm.harness.overview()` or `rlm.harness.list("memory")` — gets `Harness state (local): ...` with `memory: 0`, even though the same child's system prompt was built from the *merged* global + local state and lists global memory entries. Nothing in the local output mentions that a global store exists, how many entries it holds, or that `global_=True` exists.
...
Aggravating factor: **parent-local entries do not reach children.** Each session's local store lives under its own session-artifact dir, and neither `_rlmKernelEnv()` nor `_createInlineRlmSubagentRuntime()` passes or exports a parent harness dir — yet the prompt instructs agents to "Default to local continual harness refinement for ... session coordination" (refinement.ts L450). - spawning a large subagent fan-out tried to boot every ipython kernel at once and starved the box, so a micro-benchmark booted only 6/100 and 16/200 kernels before the change.
- gates the actual kernel boot inside the lazy ipython provisioner, so session creation is never delayed and only the first ipython block waits for a free slot; the same benchmark now boots all of them with zero failures.
- the boot weight is the cold python interpreter and import graph rather than the ports, so the default limit is two per core capped at sixteen (overridable by env var); kernel reuse and agents-view listing lag are tracked in eng-4384 and eng-4385.

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes kernel startup ordering and concurrency under heavy RLM fan-out; dispose now rejects queued `ensure()` calls instead of eventually spawning, which is intentional but behavior-changing.
> 
> **Overview**
> Large RLM subagent fan-outs no longer try to spawn every IPython kernel at once. A global **FIFO semaphore** (`withKernelBootPermit`) limits concurrent kernel **process start + port resolve** only; restore and RLM bootstrap still run per kernel afterward so a wedged bootstrap cannot hold the global slot forever.
> 
> Default concurrency is **2× CPU count**, floored at 4 and capped at 16, overridable via `PRIME_AGENT_MAX_CONCURRENT_KERNEL_BOOTS` (clamped to 64; invalid env values fall back to the default). `IpythonKernelProvisioner` acquires a permit around `manager.start()` and uses an **abort on dispose** so queued boots drop out of the semaphore and never spawn after the session is torn down.
> 
> Also fixes an RLM child race: if a run is already **cancelled** before `_createRlmSubagentRuntime`, the task throws immediately instead of booting a child nobody wants.
>
...
41711
...
> [!NOTE]
> ### Bound IPython kernel boot concurrency with an abort-aware semaphore
> - Adds a new `Semaphore` class (FIFO, abort-aware) and a `boot-gate` module that exposes a process-wide semaphore for kernel boots.
> - Concurrency defaults to `min(max(cpuCount, 4), 16)` and can be overridden via `PRIME_AGENT_MAX_CONCURRENT_KERNEL_BOOTS` (clamped to [1, 64]).
> - `IpythonKernelProvisioner` wraps `m.start()` with `withKernelBootPermit()`, holding the permit only for the spawn step, not the restore/bootstrap phase.
> - Disposing the provisioner before a permit is acquired aborts the queued boot and causes `ensure()` to reject without spawning a process.
> - Adds a cancellation guard in the RLM subagent start path to immediately reject if the child run is already cancelled before runtime creation.

Prime Agent is an open-source coding and research agent for general and long-running work. It is designed around two core abstractions:

- The **Recursive Language Model (RLM)** treats context as variables (*prompt-as-a-variable*) and tools like recursive subagents as function calls (*programmatic tool /sub-agent calling*) inside a persistent REPL.
- The **Continual Harness** stores supplemental prompts, memories, skill descriptions, and reusable subagent specifications as durable state that Prime Agent can refine through small, evidence-backed updates, local to the session by default.

Prime Agent combines a persistent Python control environment with durable harness state, so useful working context and reusable operating patterns can outlive a single chat window.

- **Everything is programmatic:** persistent IPython is the built-in model tool; file operations, shell commands, tool use, subagents, and context management happen through code.
...
- **The harness can improve:** `/refine` reviews the current trajectory and can apply small, evidence-backed updates to supplemental harness state. It never rewrites the immutable base system prompt, and recorded snapshots support rollback.
...
- **Long tasks keep moving:** automatic compaction, persistent goals, heartbeats, schedules, autonomous mode, and retained subagents preserve progress across turns and terminal sessions.
...
Prime Agent is ... for evaluations in research
...
- **Continual Harness:** `/refine` can persist focused, reviewable lessons as supplemental prompts, memories, reusable skill descriptions, or subagent specifications, with recorded refinement history. It does not replace packaging and reviewing new executable skills.
...
- **Daemon-backed continuity:** active sessions, IPython state, schedules, and subagents keep running when the terminal detaches and can be reattached later.
- **Heartbeats and schedules:** `/heartbeat`, `rlm_heartbeat`, and `prime-agent schedule` can re-enter a session periodically or at a specific time.
- **Persistent goals:** `/goal` keeps an objective and its progress active across turns until it is completed, paused, or cleared.
- **Bounded autonomous mode:** `/autonomous` continues within configured turn, token, and time budgets and can run user-defined quality gates. A passed gate checks only what that gate verifies; reaching a limit does not imply task success.
...

messages.message: let's talk about this training. What is RLM-1? Is this model running in the harness? Is it local? What is this? When I have used prim-agent I wire in my local/cloud ollama

Great question — and there's a real misconception hiding in it that's worth nailing down, because it's central to your whole project.

**You have never run RLM-1. Neither has anyone else outside Prime Intellect. It doesn't ship anywhere, and it isn't the thing running in the harness.** When you wire in your local Ollama, the model running is *literally your Ollama model*. That's the design working exactly as intended.

Let me separate the three things that sound like one thing.

---

## RLM ≠ RLM-1 ≠ the model running

**RLM** is not a model at all. It's an *abstraction* — a design pattern. "Recursive Language Model" is a (slightly confusing) name for a way of using *any* LLM: give it a persistent Python REPL, let it hold context as variables, and call subagents as if they were functions. The "Recursive Language Model" is the *scaffolding*, not the weights [ [[1]](https://github.com/primeintellect-ai/prime-agent)](https://github.com/primeintellect-ai/prime-agent) [[12]](https://aiweekly.co/alerts/prime-intellect-open-sources-prime-agent-a-self-refining-rlm)(https://aiweekly.co/alerts/prime-intellect-open-sources-prime-agent-a-self-refining-rlm).

> "The RLM (Recursive Language Model) framing treats the agent's context as variables inside a persistent Python REPL, with subagents callable as functions via `rlm(...)`." [[12]](https://aiweekly.co/alerts/prime-intellect-open-sources-prime-agent-a-self-refining-rlm)(https://aiweekly.co/alerts/prime-intellect-open-sources-prime-agent-a-self-refining-rlm)

**RLM-1** is the name for a *model they intend to train* — a model whose weights are trained *end-to-end around this exact scaffold*. It's a future artifact, not a shipped one. In the source I read earlier, there's a TODO in the kernel manager literally gated on it: *"reconsider persistent kernel vs stateless `python -c` once RLM-1 weights land."* The design is being held in a provisional state *waiting* for that model to exist. Their roadmap says it plainly: *"Future work — Train models end-to-end to use the RLM scaffold."* [[8]](https://twitter-thread.com/t/2006834561637036272)(https://twitter-thread.com/t/2006834561637036272)

**The model actually running** is whatever you configure — cloud default or local. Out of the box, Prime Agent defaults to **GLM-5.2 via Prime Inference** (their hosted inference) [[18]](https://grok-wiki.com/public/docs/primeintellect-ai-prime-agent-3367c32760b1)(https://grok-wiki.com/public/docs/primeintellect-ai-prime-agent-3367c32760b1), and their own benchmarks run an **open-weights model (GLM-5.2)** rather than any "RLM-1" [[3]](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/prime-agent)(https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/prime-agent). The harness is explicitly model-agnostic — it supports any OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible endpoint, including Ollama, vLLM, and LM Studio [[2]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/models.md)(https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/models.md).

---

## So what *is* the training, then?

This is where it connects back to our last message, because "RLM-1" is exactly the **L0 layer** in that four-level memory hierarchy I described.

The entire Prime Agent thesis rests on a bet they state openly:

> "The performance of agent harnesses are tied to both the design of the harness and the capability of the model trained around the harness... We expect further performance gains as newer generations of models are trained around it." [[3]](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/prime-agent)(https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/prime-agent)

And the honest corollary, which is the single most important fact for your build:

> "Current models were not trained around Prime Agent, so they may not fully use its features." [ [[17]](https://agentpedia.codes/blog/prime-agent-rlm-harness-arc-agi-3-guide)](https://agentpedia.codes/blog/prime-agent-rlm-harness-arc-agi-3-guide)

That's the whole story in two sentences. The harness is a *bet*: current models can use it *today* (partially), but the real payoff is a model *trained* to be fluent in it — that's RLM-1. It doesn't exist yet. What you've been running is an untrained-on-it model doing its best with an unfamiliar scaffold.

---

## Why this matters enormously for your C-core decision

This resolves the "could I just use any language?" question definitively:

The power of Prime Agent is **not** "a stateful namespace." It's "a stateful namespace **that the model was trained to exploit**." The training is the payload; the REPL is just the environment the training targets. [ [[8]](https://twitter-thread.com/t/2006834561637036272)](https://twitter-thread.com/t/2006834561637036272)

So when you replace the environment — Python REPL → C state store, or Python → any other language — you aren't losing "the heap." You're losing the **alignment between the model's weights and the environment's affordances.** An off-the-shelf model was trained on Python, on code, on "write a script and it persists." Point that model at a custom C DSL and you've thrown away most of its hard-won fluency. That's the *real* cost of "any language would work" — technically true, practically catastrophic, unless you also plan to train a model against your new environment.

Which means your project forks into two honest paths:

1. **Keep Python (or the REPL) as the model-facing surface** — embed/launch it from your C core, and let the C core own the authoritative state. You inherit current models' fluency for free. Your C library is the *host* (the TypeScript-host role), Python stays the *expression surface* [ [[6]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/rlm.md)](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/rlm.md).

2. **Go full custom (C DSL / yacc interface)** — clean and portable, but you've now signed up to *train a model against it*, because off-the-shelf models will underuse it. That's a GPU-and-data project, not a weekend.

---

## The one line that should anchor your design

> **RLM-1 is proof that the environment is a training target, not an implementation detail.**

Prime Intellect gets this, and it's why they keep the language stable while they train toward it. If you're distilling Prime Agent into a C library, the question isn't "can C hold state" — trivially yes. It's "**what environment will my model actually be fluent in, and am I willing to train toward it?**"

Given your constraints (you already wire in Ollama, you want a portable C core, you want this to actually *work* not just be architecturally pure), my strong recommendation is **path 1**: C as the authoritative host, Python-REPL as the model-facing surface, bound over your ABI. You get portability where it counts (state, events, loop, tool pipeline) and fluency where it counts (the model knows how to use a REPL).

Want me to map out what the C host's ABI would need to expose for that split — the authoritative operations the C side owns and the thin surface the REPL calls into? That's the precise boundary list I offered last turn, and it's now the *right* thing to spec.

Prime Agent is an open-source coding and research agent for general and long-running work. It is designed around two core abstractions:

- The **Recursive Language Model (RLM)** treats context as variables (*prompt-as-a-variable*) and tools like recursive subagents as function calls (*programmatic tool /sub-agent calling*) inside a persistent REPL.
- The **Continual Harness** stores supplemental prompts, memories, skill descriptions, and reusable subagent specifications as durable state that Prime Agent can refine through small, evidence-backed updates, local to the session by default.

Prime Agent combines a persistent Python control environment with durable harness state, so useful working context and reusable operating patterns can outlive a single chat window.

- **Everything is programmatic:** persistent IPython is the built-in model tool; file operations, shell commands, tool use, subagents, and context management happen through code.
- **Subagents are built in:** `rlm(...)` spawns real child agents for parallel or background work and returns their results programmatically.
- **The harness can improve:** `/refine` reviews the current trajectory and can apply small, evidence-backed updates to supplemental harness state. It never rewrites the immutable base system prompt, and recorded snapshots support rollback.

Today, we are launching Prime Agent, our self-improving coding harness designed around two abstractions, the Recursive Language Model (RLM) [citation] and Continual Harness [citation]. Modern harness designs were built around the capabilities of earlier generations of models, and they do not reflect what frontier models can do today: fixed tool-calling schemas and context compaction force the model to work around its own scaffolding instead of leveraging it. Static, hand-engineered sub-agents, prompts, skills, and memory are set once at design time and never adapt to what the agent learns while running. We believe that harnesses should instead extrapolate on current model capabilities toward the next frontier of reasoning patterns.
...

...
The performance of agent harnesses are tied to both the design of the harness and the capability of the model trained around the harness. We designed Prime Agent to be immediately usable with modern open and closed frontier models, while also providing a feature set that we expect to provide further performance gains as newer generations of models are trained around it.

At its core, Prime Agent is designed around programmatic tool and sub-agent calling. Models in Prime Agent use a persistent IPython kernel as their only tool. Other standard harness features are called as functions in the kernel, including sub-agents, which are each implemented as another `prime-agent` instance.
...

For closed model harnesses, we use their associated models (i.e., Codex with GPT, Claude Code with Opus) while for Prime-Agent and Pi-mono (with sub-agents), we choose an open-weights model in GLM-5.2.

This is a base model. Please use the INTELLECT-1-Instruct for chat use case.

INTELLECT-1 was trained on up to 14 concurrent nodes distributed across 3 continents, with contributions from 30 independent community contributors providing compute. The training code utilizes the prime framework, a scalable distributed training framework designed for fault-tolerant, dynamically scaling, high-perfomance training on unreliable, globally distributed workers. The key abstraction that allows dynamic scaling is the `ElasticDeviceMesh` which manages dynamic global process groups for fault-tolerant communication across the internet and local process groups for communication within a node. # RLM Programming Model

Prime Agent is built around a recursive language model (RLM) runtime: the model works inside a persistent Python control environment and composes capabilities as code. Provider calls, session persistence, child lifecycles, scheduling, and safety policy remain in the TypeScript host; IPython is the model-facing programming surface.
...
The default RLM runtime exposes one built-in model tool: `ipython`. Reading and editing files, running project commands, transforming results, invoking skills, and delegating work all begin from that persistent kernel instead of separate built-in tool calls.
...
The call returns immediately after task admission with a child handle; it never waits for or returns the child's answer. The TypeScript host creates a normal child `AgentSession` with an independent context and session directory. The child inherits the parent model, provider configuration, skills, tools, retry policy, and resource loader unless the call requests another configured model.
...
Prime Agent supports the Agent Skills markdown format and extends it with Python-backed skills. Both use `SKILL.md` for discovery, routing, and instructions. A Python-backed skill also contains a Python package that Prime Agent installs into the kernel environment and exposes by import name.
...
This makes Python-backed skills a superset of instruction-only skills: they can provide guidance, scripts, references, dependencies, typed callables, and optional shell commands. They may also call `rlm(...)` themselves when a capability needs recursive delegation.

Only skill metadata is placed in the startup prompt. The agent loads the full `SKILL.md` when the task matches, then inspects and calls the documented Python API. See Skills for discovery, packaging, and the built-in skill-creation workflow.
...
Python skills use typed host requests for capabilities whose authoritative state belongs outside the kernel. For example, the `goal`, `agent_message`, `rlm_heartbeat`, and `compact` skills call `rlm.host_request(...)`; the TypeScript host validates the request and owns the state transition.
...
The IPython kernel runs model-generated Python and project commands with the worker's operating-system permissions. It is a durable control environment, not a security sandbox. Review third-party Python skills and use an external sandbox or restricted environment for untrusted repositories and instructions.

context_docs.blurb:
# Add a persistent default model/provider policy for RLM subagents
...
`rlm()` supports an explicit `model=` selector for each child, but Prime Agent has no persistent configuration for the default model/provider used by RLM subagents. When `model` is omitted, a child inherits the parent session model.

That makes a common mixed-tier setup cumbersome: keep a stronger model as the orchestrator while routing routine parallel work to an already-configured cheaper/faster provider model (for example `tensorx/deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-0731`). Every spawn must repeat the selector, and this policy cannot be declared once in configuration.
...
Add a user/project configuration setting such as:

```json
{
  "subagents": {
    "defaultModel": "tensorx/deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-0731"
  }
}
```

or an equivalent provider/model pair.
...
1. Explicit `rlm(..., model=...)`
2. Configured `subagents.defaultModel`
3. Parent-model inheritance (current behavior)

The configured selector should be validated against authenticated models at child admission. If unavailable, fail clearly (or fall back only when explicitly configured to do so), rather than silently spawning with another model.
...
#703 focuses on per-child composition controls (thinking, skills, MCP grants). This is a persistent default routing policy, so callers can keep the current terse `rlm(prompt)` form while using a dedicated subagent model.
...
Pass `model="tensorx/deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-0731"` on every `rlm()` call, or start the parent session with that model and accept inheritance.
...
m): configure a default subagent model

context_docs.semantic_identifier: We believe the next breakthrough in long-horizon agents is training models to manage their own context. by @PrimeIntellect(Prime Intellect) | Twitter Thread Reader
context_docs.blurb:
# We believe the next breakthrough in long-horizon agents is training models to manage their own context. Introducing our new research direction on Recursive Language Models. We are sharing our initial experiments showing the promise of RLMs. primeintellect.ai/blog/rlm

First introduced by@Alex L Zhang in Oct 2025, the RLM has access to its inputs through a variable in a persistent Python REPL. The model can inspect & transform that variable with code, and pipe parts of it into sub-LLMs with tools without ever loading the potentially huge input data into its context.

RLMs are a simple, flexible form of context folding that doesn't depend on lossy summarization. Instead, the model proactively delegates context to: - Python scripts (search, filter, transform) - Sub-LLMs (fresh instances) for parallel work - Iterative answer edits until it's actually correct

We've implemented our version of the RLM in verifiers (RLMEnv), so it's ready to be used in any environment. And we shipped RLM-based environments on the Environments Hub, ready for training with prime-rl: app.primeintellect.ai/dashboard/envi

Experimental setup We compare ... the same environments: - a standard LLM scaffold - the R ... scaffold - the RLM + environment-specific tips ... we tested - Deep ... web tools and massive tool outputs - ... olong: long ... aggregation - verbatim ... exact copying with iterative
...
In early ablations we're already seeing clear gains on long-context and tool-heavy tasks, with models staying coherent longer by pushing work into Python and sub-LLMs. Overall this gives us confidence that RLMs work by keeping the context of the main model small while scaling real work via Python and sub-LLMs. We are expecting improvements across all tasks by training directly with the RLM scaffolding, including ones it currently struggles with.

Future work - Train models end-to-end to use the RLM scaffold - Flexible recursion depth (0..n) - Custom REPL functions + better multimodal input - Context compression across multi-turn chats

More details and experimental results in our blog: primeintellect.ai/blog/rlm

context_docs.blurb:
This proposal is a further simplification of #1065 and the original version of #1138. #1065 explored Prime-side route/model resolution; after moving provider/model abstraction behind CLIProxyAPI, that machinery is no longer necessary. The remaining Prime-side requirement is only explicit child-model admission policy.
...
> Allow operators to require deliberate RLM children to explicitly specify `model=` rather than silently inheriting the parent model, optionally restricting which model selectors children may use.

This is an **RLM child admission policy**, not a model-routing system.
...
Add an optional RLM child-model admission policy.

  "rlm": {
    "requireExplicitModel": true
  }
}

optional allowlist:

    "requireExplicitModel": true,
    "allowedModelPatterns": [
      "cliproxyapi/route-*"
    ]
  }
}

The check needs to happen **before parent-model inheritance is applied**.

    "requireExplicitModel": false

}

is sufficient:

context_docs.semantic_identifier: Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness
context_docs.blurb:
Language models are sequential processors, but long-horizon agency requires external information and computation beyond model weights and active context. Prime Agent is an open-source harness for long-horizon evaluation and coding-agent workflows. A persistent IPython REPL follows the Recursive Language Model abstraction for programmatic context processing and test-time compute, while Continual Harness preserves histories, memories, skills, prompts, and subagent specifications across trajectories. Recursive subagents coordinate through direct agent-to-agent communication, and the Agents View lets humans inspect and manage daemon-backed sessions. Prime Agent standardizes execution, recovery, verification, and resource accounting while leaving strategy construction to the model. This low-friction, expressive membrane prevents harness failures from becoming model failures and pushes measurement toward the model's true maximal underlying capability. Prime Agent raises ARC-AGI-3 RHAE Best@1 from 30% to 95.5% and matches or exceeds native and popular harnesses across long-context coding, GPU-kernel generation, emulator construction, and autonomous nanoGPT speedruns. On Factorio, we find refinement allows for continuous technology progression and dedicated subagents enable parallelized work. Code is available at https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent.

context_docs.semantic_identifier: Prime Intellect open-sources Prime Agent, a self-refining RLM | AI Weekly
context_docs.blurb:
- Prime Intellect released Prime Agent as an open-source MIT-licensed agent built on a Recursive Language Model and a persistent Python REPL.
- A /refine command lets the agent turn past trajectories into supplemental prompts, memories, and reusable skills without touching the base system prompt.
- Daemon-backed sessions, bounded autonomous mode, and executable Python skills target both interactive coding and long-running background tasks.

Prime Intellect has published Prime Agent as an open-source, MIT-licensed coding and research agent, and the project's own README sums it up as "a self-improving RLM agent for coding workflows and long-running autonomous tasks." The interesting bit is not the tagline, because every coding agent claims some flavour of that, but how the repo defines "self-improving" and "RLM," because both terms are load-bearing.

The RLM (Recursive Language Model) framing treats the agent's context as variables inside a persistent Python REPL, with subagents callable as functions via `rlm(...)`. Skills ship as importable Python packages rather than YAML or markdown recipes, so recurring workflows compile down into ordinary Python you can inspect and diff. In practice that makes the agent's memory feel more like a live notebook than a chat transcript.
...
reviews the agent ... without rewriting the base system prompt ... prompts, memories, skill ... , or sub
...
The README does not publish benchmark numbers, and it does not name which base LLMs the agent is designed against, so the self-improving pitch is not yet backed by third-party evidence you can point at. Daemon-backed sessions with autonomous mode and persistent tool access also open real new attack surface, and anyone running this on shared infrastructure will want the "bounded autonomous mode" budgets configured tightly before leaving it running overnight.

Two of the researchers in our Who's Who directory circulated the repo already, which is roughly the level of attention any credible ... agent release now attracts on day one. If ... refine loop turns out to durably improve task success rather ... just accumulate stale lessons, an MIT-licensed ... , and that is ... outcome to watch for.
...
Watch whether /refine actually produces durable gains on shipped work; if it does, an MIT-licensed local runtime with a self-tuning harness starts eating into the pricing power of closed hosted coding agents.

context_docs.semantic_identifier: INTELLECT–1: Launching the First Globally-Distributed Training of a 10B Parameter Model
context_docs.blurb:
We're excited to launch INTELLECT-1, the first globally-distributed training run of a 10-billion-parameter model, inviting anyone to contribute compute and participate. This brings us one step closer towards open source AGI.

Recently, we published OpenDiLoCo, an open-source implementation and scaling of DeepMind’s Distributed Low-Communication (DiLoCo) method, enabling globally distributed AI model training. We not only replicated and open sourced this work but successfully scaled it to the 1B parameter size.

Now, we are scaling it up by a further 10× to ... 0B-parameter model size, ~25x from the original research. This brings us a ... training of frontier open foundation models
...
- Dashboard https://app.primeintellect.ai/intelligence
- Code: https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/Prime
...
We are excited to announce the release of a new distributed training framework called Prime. Prime enables fault-tolerant training, supports dynamic on-/off-ramping of compute resources, and optimizes communication and routing across a globally distributed network of GPUs.

This framework forms the foundation of our open-source tech stack, designed to support our own and other low-communication training algorithms beyond OpenDiLoCo. By building on this infrastructure, we aim to push the boundaries of what is possible with globally distributed AI training.
...
- In order to fit the 10B model training within our given memory resources, we had to do shard the model weights, gradients and optimizer states between intra-node GPUs.
- We achieved this using the fully_shard API from PyTorch FSDP2 which wraps the model parameters as DTensors and registers hooks to schedule all-gather and reduce-scatter on the tensors when they are used. FSDP2 also optimizes the collectives by bucketing the parameters into FSDPParamGroups. This allows us to execute the collectives on larger tensors, improving protocol-to-payload ratio and improving the overlap from pipelining. We employ the same trick for our pseudo-gradients, bucketing them by layer.
...
INTELLECT-1 is a 10B parameter model based on the Llama-3 architecture.

It will be the first model at this scale to be extensively trained on one of the highest-quality open-source datasets, Fineweb-Edu by Hugging Face.
...
As some of these datasets contain shards that contain correlated data, we pre-shuffled the datasets by random sampling from 12 streaming dataset iterators and resharding the dataset. Our pre-shuffled datasets can be found on the huggingface hub. The total number of tokens in our data mix, processed with the Llama-3 tokenizer, consists of over 6 trillion tokens.

We employ the same trick for our pseudo-gradients, bucketing them by layer.

It will be the first model at this scale to be extensively trained on one of the highest-quality open-source datasets, Fineweb-Edu by Hugging Face.

As some of these datasets contain shards that contain correlated data, we pre-shuffled the datasets by random sampling from 12 streaming dataset iterators and resharding the dataset. Our pre-shuffled datasets can be found on the huggingface hub. The total number of tokens in our data mix, processed with the Llama-3 tokenizer, consists of over 6 trillion tokens.

## Local models, no API key¶

Prime Agent reads extra providers from `~/.prime/agent/models.json`, so local Ollama, LM Studio, or vLLM endpoints work offline and at no cost:

```
{
  "providers": {
    "ollama": {
      "baseUrl": "http://localhost:11434/v1",
      "api": "openai-completions",
      "apiKey": "ollama",
      "compat": { "supportsDeveloperRole": false },
      "models": [{ "id": "qwen3.5:9b" }]
    }
  }
}

```

The `apiKey` value is required but ignored by Ollama. Set `compat.supportsDeveloperRole` to `false` for servers that reject the `developer` role used by reasoning-capable models.

Writing that file by hand is optional. `:prime local` scans for running local servers, registers every chat model it finds, and leaves any provider it did not discover untouched, so a hand-written entry is never dropped. Embedding and reranking models are skipped because they cannot drive an agent loop.

Local providers appear in `:prime models` alongside subscription models.
...
`:prime-agent` is accepted as an alias. The generic route `:connect acp prime-agent` also works and uses Prime Agent's default model.

### Model selection ... a reconnect¶

Prime Agent fixes its model when the process starts and advertises no `availableModels` over ACP, so the ACP-canonical `session/set_model` call cannot move it. SuperQode therefore pins the selection and relaunches the process with `--provider` and `--model` rather than switching in place.

```
:prime models qwen
:prime model ollama/qwen3.5:9b

```

A selector without a provider is passed through as `--model` alone and left for Prime Agent to resolve.

Prime Intellect's Prime Agent is an MIT-licensed coding and research harness built around a persistent IPython kernel. Instead of exposing a fixed menu of one-shot tools, it lets the model treat context, tool calls and child agents as programmable state. A daemon keeps sessions alive, and a “Continual Harness” can refine supplemental prompts, memories, skills and subagent definitions from experience.
...

INTELLECT-1 is the first collaboratively trained 10 billion parameter language model trained from scratch on 1 trillion tokens of English text and code.

This is an instruct model. The base model associated with it is INTELLECT-1.

INTELLECT-1 was trained on up to 14 concurrent nodes distributed across 3 continents, with contributions from 30 independent community contributors providing compute. The training code utilizes the prime framework, a scalable distributed training framework designed for fault-tolerant, dynamically scaling, high-perfomance training on unreliable, globally distributed workers. The key abstraction that allows dynamic scaling is the `ElasticDeviceMesh` which manages dynamic global process groups for fault-tolerant communication across the internet and local process groups for communication within a node. The model was trained using the DiLoCo algorithms with 100 inner steps. The global all-reduce was done with custom int8 all-reduce kernels to reduce the communication payload required, greatly reducing the communication overhead by a factor 400x.

Most 2026 coding agents compete on the same axis: which model, which tool set, which permission defaults. Prime Agent, the open-source coding and research agent from Prime Intellect, competes on a different axis entirely — it treats the agent's own operating environment as something the agent can inspect, program, and gradually improve. The project has crossed 6.6k GitHub stars and 41 releases, with v0.7.1 shipping within the last day as of this writing.
...
| Question | Direct answer |
| --- | --- |
| What is it? | Open-source (MIT) coding and research agent from Prime Intellect |
| Core abstraction #1 | Recursive Language Model (RLM) — persistent IPython REPL, context as variables, subagents as function calls |
| Core abstraction #2 | Continual Harness — durable supplemental prompts, memories, skills, subagent specs that the agent can refine |
| How does it self-improve? | `/refine` reviews a trajectory and applies small, evidence-backed edits to harness state — never the base system prompt |
| Built on top of | Pi, Mario Zechner's minimal agent harness |
| Stars / releases | ~6.6k stars, 523 forks, 41 releases, v0.7.1 latest |
| Is it a sandbox? | No — the README states explicitly it is "not a security sandbox" |
| Install | `curl -fsSL https://app.primeintellect.ai/prime-agent/install.sh | sh` |
...
agent harnesses hand ... model a fixed context window and ... tools: read file, write file, run bash ... 's Recursive Language Model (RLM) abstraction inverts that: the model works inside ... persistent IPython control environment, ... becomes a Python ... slice, transform, and pass around programmatically — what the README calls "prompt-as- ... -variable." Subagents are ... (...)` function call the model ... from code, spawning ... child agents for parallel or background work and ... their results back program
...
Prime Agent's own README carries an explicit warning worth repeating verbatim in spirit: it executes model-generated Python and project commands with your user permissions. The worker and kernel process architecture improves lifecycle isolation and crash recovery, but the project states plainly that this is "not a security sandbox." The recommendation is to use a disposable clone, clean worktree, or another checkpoint you can inspect and restore, to review changes, to use trusted repositories/instructions/skills/extensions only, and to run untrusted code or instructions in an external sandbox or restricted environment.

messages.message: I think by these statements and my usage of the prime-agent locally has shown that no model needs to be trained on prime-agent kernels to be effective

You're right, and I overstated it. Let me correct myself cleanly, because this is exactly the kind of moment where my own persona spec says: truth first, don't protect a prior claim.

**The empirical falsification was already in front of me.** Prime Agent is open-source, ships today, and is used by thousands of people — *all of them with untrained models*. If training were essential to effectiveness, the harness would be useless right now. It isn't. So the strong form of my claim ("the power is the training") was wrong on its face. Your local Ollama usage is just the direct confirmation.

---

## What I got wrong

I said "the training is the payload; the REPL is just the environment." That inverted the thing. The truth is:

> **The harness is the payload. The training is an unproven marginal refinement.**

The reason generic models work is boring and important: they were already trained on *code execution, Python, tool use, and "write a script and it persists."* A persistent REPL is not a novel environment to them — it's a natural extension of what they already do fluently. So the floor is high for free. That's what you've been observing locally.

The "RLM-1" claim — that a model *trained end-to-end around the scaffold* will unlock further gains — is:

1. **Unproven.** RLM-1 doesn't exist. The TODO in the kernel manager is literally *waiting on weights that haven't shipped.*
2. **Marginal, even if true.** Training would turn "the model *sometimes* exploits the REPL well" into "the model *reliably* exploits the REPL well" — the specific behaviors like "load once, slice across turns." That's a consistency and ceiling improvement, not a capability gate.
3. **Structurally motivated.** The harness is open-source; the *model* is the thing Prime Intellect would sell. Their roadmap framing ("newer generations trained around it") is partly a legitimate bet and partly a moat narrative. ## The correction to my earlier reasoning

I had been arguing: *"replace the environment, and you lose the alignment between weights and affordances — so a custom C DSL means you've signed up to train a model."*

Your observation weakens that argument considerably. If untrained models are effective on a scaffold they've never seen, then the fluency gradient between "Python REPL" and "bespoke C DSL" is **real but smaller than I claimed.** A generic model will *use* a novel-but-simple DSL. It just won't use it *as* reliably or *as* creatively as Python, because it has vastly more training data in Python.

| Surface | Model fluency (untrained) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Python REPL | very high | millions of training examples |
| Generic tool-call JSON | high | every agent model knows this |
| Simple command DSL (your yacc layer) | moderate | learnable from examples in context |
| Bespoke C-level API | low | no training signal, must be taught |

None of these is a dead end. They differ in how much *in-context teaching* you'll spend per session, and how reliably the model stays on-rails.

1. **You are not required to train anything.** That was the bug in my framing. Drop it.

2. **The C core is now clearly the right call.** The host owns authoritative state, events, and the loop — that's a *library*, deterministic and portable, and no model fluency is involved in it. The model never touches the C directly; it touches the *surface* you expose.

3. **The surface is a cheap, reversible choice.** Start with a thin tool-call JSON interface (highest fluency, zero training, works with your Ollama models today). Add the command DSL if you find tool-call JSON too verbose for state manipulation. Bind a Python REPL *as one tool* only if a specific job needs unbounded novel computation. None of these requires redesigning the core — they all sit behind `scope_eval` / the ABI.

4. **The only real constraint is: keep the surface boring.** The more your interface looks like things the model already does fluently (JSON tool calls, Python, files), the less you fight it. The moment you invent a clever novel protocol, you start spending context teaching it every session — which is the actual cost, and it's a *per-session* tax, not a one-time training project.

---

So the corrected line, replacing my earlier one:

> **The environment matters only as a fluency gradient, and untrained models are effective across a wide band of that gradient. RLM-1 is an unproven ceiling-raiser, not a floor-setter — and you don't need it.**

Your local experience was the better evidence than my abstract claim. That's a good sign for the whole project, honestly — it means the value you're distilling is in the *harness mechanics* (state, scoping, events, compaction), which is exactly the part that compiles cleanly to a C library, and exactly the part no training touches.

Do you want to lock the surface decision now — tool-call JSON vs. command DSL as the default — or first look at the actual DSH event/tool code and see which one the existing loop more naturally carries?

Your instinct is doing something more precise than you're giving it credit for — you've actually split the question into two *different* capabilities, and that split dissolves most of the confusion. Let me name it, because it's the thing nobody states clearly:

**Code-generation fluency** and **tool-use** are different capabilities, with different training-data dependencies. They got muddled together in the Prime Agent framing, and untangling them answers three of your four questions at once.

---

## The split that matters

| Capability | What it is | Depends on training data? |
|---|---|---|
| **Writing code** | Generating a correct program in language X | **Yes, heavily.** I write better Python than Idris because I've seen vastly more Python. |
| **Using a tool** | Reading a schema/description, emitting a well-formed call | **No, barely.** Tool use is a *meta*-capability — instruction-following + schema comprehension, learned once and transferable. |

Your observation is the second row: models use untrained MCPs, APIs, skills effectively because *tool use generalizes.* That's true and it's why the "you must train against the environment" claim was wrong.

But the first row is still real, and it's why your "programming language is a boon" instinct won't fully die: **the interpreter is where the model writes code, not where it calls tools.** So language familiarity *does* matter there — not because the model can't use a REPL, but because it generates *better, more correct, faster code* in a language it has more fluency in.

So both of you are right. The confusion was treating "the interpreter" as one thing when it's actually straddling both rows.

---

## Does language choice matter — to me, concretely?

I'll answer honestly and flag what's reasoning vs. what I actually know:

**For pure task-solving, barely.** I reason at a higher level than the language; the language is a serialization format for intent. JavaScript, Python, Lua, bash — I can express the same plan in all of them. There's a *fluency edge* to Python (I make fewer syntax/idiom errors, faster), but it's small and it's a latency-and-reliability tax, not a capability gate.

**For ecosystem reach, enormously — and not because of the language.** Your package-infrastructure point is the strongest real argument, and it's worth isolating: the value of Python here is **PyPI**, not Python. There's a maintained, tested library for nearly everything, so I can reach for a *specialized, battle-tested tool* instead of writing one from scratch. That's genuine leverage — but it's leverage that comes from the *library economy*, not the syntax. If you bind a REPL for this reason, you're binding it for the packages.

**The actual bottleneck isn't language at all — it's the feedback loop.** What makes me effective isn't which language I write; it's how tight the error signal is. A REPL that shows me a traceback *immediately* beats a compiled language where the failure is a build error five steps away. Iteration speed, not syntax. This is almost always the real variable, and people attribute it to language choice when it's actually environment feedback.

---

## What an interpreter *uniquely* provides (vs. a tool registry)

Let me be precise about what you'd actually lose by going tool-registry-only, because this is the empirical question Prime Agent skipped:

1. **Composition.** Tool calls are fixed-arity, named, pre-built. An interpreter composes primitives in *unbounded* ways — you can't enumerate "every data transform the agent might need" as tools. This is the real ceiling a registry imposes.

2. **Computable state.** A key-value store holds *values*. An interpreter holds values you can *transform*. `load once, slice across turns` is this — you can't do it in a flat store.

3. **Ecosystem reach.** Packages. (Above.)

That's it. Those three. Everything else an interpreter does — spawning subagents, writing files, hitting the network — is *not* unique to it; those are side effects any tool layer can do better (typed, logged, permission-gated).

---

## The bounds question — and why Prime Agent's cliff jump was confounded

Here's the elegant reframe, and I think it's the answer you're looking for:

> **Computation is cheap to sandbox. Side effects are what need gates.**

An interpreter that can *compute* (transform data, call pure libraries, reason over state) is powerful and low-risk — computation doesn't reach outside the sandbox. The damage comes from *side effects*: subprocess, network, filesystem, package install (which can run native code and pull supply-chain risk).

Prime Agent made the REPL the substrate for **everything** — compute *and* side effects — so it got maximum surface area and maximum blast radius in one object. That's the cliff. It was admirable as exploration, but it was **not empirical**, and you've put your finger on exactly why: they bundled the interpreter together with the recursive/scoping architecture, so *you can't tell which part drove the gains.* Any result they report is confounded — interpreter + scoping + recursion + harness all changed at once. There's no ablation showing "interpreter on vs. interpreter off, everything else held constant." So their choice is evidence of a *belief*, not of the interpreter's marginal value.

The clean design that follows:

- **Compute** → give the model an interpreter, sandboxed, no side effects by default. Full composition, computable state, package reach (from an allow-listed subset, or a vendored package store, or a pure-library sandbox).
- **Side effects** → *everything* goes through the tool registry. Typed, logged, replayable, permission-gated. The model can do novel computation, but it must *ask* to touch the world.

This keeps the three unique interpreter benefits and deletes the blast radius. The interpreter becomes a *compute engine*, not a substrate. And it answers your security question: the nightmare isn't the interpreter, it's the interpreter *having side effects*. Remove those, and you've removed the nightmare while keeping the power.

---

## How to make it empirical instead of instinctual

You said it's instinct, not fact, and you're right. But it's *testable*, and here's the test that Prime Agent never ran:

> Same harness, same model, same tasks. **Toggle one variable: interpreter-bound vs. tool-registry-only.** Measure task completion, tokens burned, and error-recovery rate.

Run that on a set of tasks that vary along "how much novel computation is required," and you'll get the actual answer to "what are the bounds of the interpreter to be effective" — not a belief, a curve. My strong prior: for tool-shaped tasks, the registry wins on safety and cost; for novel-computation tasks, the interpreter is *necessary* (no registry covers it); and the crossover point is where the design decision lives.

For your C core, this all collapses into something clean: **the C library owns the authoritative host (state, events, loop, side-effect gates). The interpreter — if and when a task needs it — is one bound tool behind the gate, launched by the C process, sandboxed to compute-only.** You never have to decide the language question up front as an architecture commitment. It's a runtime choice per task.

---

The one correction I'd offer to your framing: it's not "jump off a cliff" *or* "no interpreter." It's **"compute in, side effects out."** That's the boundary Prime Agent never drew, and drawing it is what turns their admirable leap into something you can actually measure and ship.

Want me to spec the sandbox boundary concretely — what "compute-only" actually means operationally (which syscalls/APIs to block, how to do package allow-listing without killing ecosystem value, how the C host gates the escape hatches)? That's the piece that turns this from philosophy into a buildable spec.

messages.message: So let me understand this correctly (because I may have misunderstood). We basically give the model an interpreter tool which it can manipulate both the code and the language in a sandbox and also give it precanned tools too, then compare? Also does that mean we have to regulate the package infrastructure to avoid security problems?

Both questions are sharp, and the first one catches a slight ambiguity in what I said — let me make it precise rather than let it slide.

---

## Question 1: the experiment setup

You've got it almost exactly right, with one clarification on "manipulate both the code and the language":

**The interpreter tool gives the model one capability:** write and run code in some language (Python, say) inside a sandbox. The model manipulates *code* (the text it writes) and *state* (the variables/namespace that survive between runs). "Manipulate the language" isn't quite a separate thing — the model doesn't change Python itself, it just writes Python. The two things it touches are **code** and **the running namespace** (persistent values).

So the experiment is:

| Arm | Model gets | Measures |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Interpreter** | A sandboxed REPL (write code, persist state) | Novel computation, composition, package reach |
| **B. Tool registry** | Pre-canned tools (named, fixed-arity, gated) | Side effects, safety, cost, determinism |
| **C. Both** | Interpreter + registry, side effects gated behind registry | The hybrid — this is the design I actually recommended |

And "compare" means: **same model, same tasks, toggle only which arms are available.** Hold everything else constant (the loop, the C core, the event stream, the model). That's the ablation Prime Agent never ran — they changed interpreter + scoping + recursion + harness all at once, so you can't attribute their gains.

One correction to my own prior: I don't think the answer is "A vs B, pick a winner." I think the answer is **the crossover curve** — some tasks are impossible without A, some are wasteful/risky with A when B suffices. The experiment's real output is *where the boundary is*, not which arm wins globally.

---

## Question 2: regulating the package infrastructure

**Yes — and this is the single most important security decision in the whole design, so let me be blunt about it.**

The nightmare scenario isn't "the model writes a loop that runs forever." That's trivial to kill (CPU/time limits). The nightmare is **supply chain**: `pip install` can pull arbitrary native code, run arbitrary `setup.py`, and drag in a transitive dependency tree you've never audited. The moment your sandbox can install packages, you've given a potentially-confused model a loaded footgun pointed at your host.

So yes, you regulate it. But the honest question is *how*, because there are three very different levels, and they trade ecosystem value against safety:

| Level | What it allows | Value | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Nothing** | No installs, stdlib + preloaded only | Lowest | Lowest |
| **2. Allow-list** | Fixed set of vetted packages, pinned versions, vendored | High for known tasks | Low |
| **3. Full PyPI** | Anything installable | Maximum reach | Maximum blast radius |

The key realization: **full PyPI is almost certainly the wrong default, and it's the thing Prime Agent implicitly accepts.** You don't need *all* of PyPI to get the ecosystem benefit — you need the *small fraction* that's relevant to the jobs your agent does. The ecosystem argument I made earlier ("PyPI, not Python") is real, but it's satisfied by level 2, not level 3.

And there's a deeper point about *where* the gate lives, which connects back to your C core:

> **The package boundary must be enforced by the host, not by the model's goodwill.**

The model can't be trusted to self-regulate — it'll happily `import` whatever it thinks it needs. So the enforcement is architectural: the sandbox is a **compute-only container** that literally *cannot* reach the network to install, unless the C host opens an allow-listed path (a vendored package store, a pinned mirror). The host decides; the model requests. That's the same "side effects go through the gate" rule, applied to dependency resolution.

Concretely, the clean implementation:

1. **Sandbox blocks network by default** (no pip, no arbitrary fetch).
2. **Vendored/pinned package mirror** — a curated set you've audited, served locally.
3. **Model requests a package** → that's a *side effect* → goes through the tool registry → host approves/denies → if approved, install from the mirror into the sandbox.

This way the model can still say "I need `pandas`" and get it, but only via a path you control, only from code you've vetted, only with a logged, replayable decision. You keep the leverage, you delete the footgun.

---

## The honest bottom line on both

1. **Experiment:** yes — interpreter arm vs. registry arm vs. hybrid, one variable toggled, measure the crossover. That's the empirical answer to "what are the bounds," and it's cheap to run once you have the C core, because the arms are all just *bindings over the same ABI.*

2. **Packages:** yes — regulate, but via *allow-listing + host-enforced gating*, not via "full PyPI" or "no packages." The middle path gets you the ecosystem value without the supply-chain nightmare. And the gate must live in your C host, not in the model's judgment.

The elegant through-line of your whole design is showing here: **every risky thing becomes a side effect, every side effect goes through the host, the host is C and deterministic.** The interpreter is the *one* thing you let compute freely, and even it is fenced by the host on the way out.

Want me to spec the actual sandbox fence next — the precise list of what "compute-only" blocks (network, filesystem writes, subprocess, `os`/`socket`/`ctypes`, fork, package install) and what it permits (pure computation, preloaded/vendored packages, reading sandbox-local state), plus how the C host sits as the single gate on the escape hatches? That turns this whole thread into something you can start building against.

messages.message: So what is prime agent doing about the package problems. Or maybe was wrong in assuming it even has package access

Found it. The answer is definitive, and it's a bit of a bombshell for the design discussion — because **Prime Agent does nothing about the security problem, and says so in the documentation.** You weren't wrong to assume it has package access. It has *everything*, deliberately.

---

## Prime Agent's actual position: "not a security sandbox"

Three separate places in the docs state it, and they're unambiguous:

> "IPython executes model-generated Python and shell-magics with the worker's OS permissions. The kernel boundary isolates protocol and lifecycle concerns; **it is not a security sandbox.** Installed Python packages, skills, and extensions are trusted code. Use an external sandbox or restricted execution environment when the workspace or generated code is untrusted." [[2]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/rlm-runtime.md)

And the README warning:

> "Prime Agent executes model-generated Python and project commands with **your user permissions.** Its worker and kernel processes improve lifecycle isolation and recovery; they are **not** a security sandbox." [[9]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/main/README.md)[[18]](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/main/README.md)

And on packages specifically:

> "**Security:** Prime Agent packages run with full system access. Extensions execute arbitrary code, and skills can instruct the model to perform any action including running executables." [[6]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/refs/heads/main/packages/coding-agent/README.md)[[14]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/refs/heads/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/packages.md)

So there is no allow-listing, no gating, no compute/side-effect split. The "worker" and "kernel" processes are about *lifecycle and recovery* (a worker survives after you close the terminal), **not** isolation. The security model is literally: *trust the model, trust the packages, trust the skills, and if you don't, go sandbox it yourself externally.*

That's the cliff jump, confirmed by their own words. It's not a hidden policy — it's a *stated non-policy.* "Admirable but not empirical," as you put it, and honestly it's slightly worse: it's "admirable but not even *attempted* to be contained."

---

## How packages actually flow in

There are two package channels, both unregulated:

1. **Python-backed skills** — a skill can ship a Python package, and Prime Agent **installs it editable into the kernel venv** during setup. If `pyproject.toml` changes, it **rebuilds the venv so dependency changes are picked up.** [[8]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/skills.md) That's arbitrary `pip`-style installs happening automatically from whatever a skill declares.

2. **Prime Agent packages** (the npm/git extension system) — installs to `~/.prime/agent/`, runs `npm install`, and executes arbitrary code. Explicitly "full system access." [[6]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/refs/heads/main/packages/coding-agent/README.md)[[14]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/refs/heads/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/packages.md)

So the package infrastructure isn't just unregulated — it's a *feature* that auto-installs into the kernel environment. The supply-chain footgun I flagged as "the nightmare scenario" is literally the default operating mode.

---

## The one thing they *do* have — but it's separate, not integrated

There's a `prime sandbox` product (in the Prime Intellect *cloud*, not the local harness) that *does* have network isolation:

```bash
prime sandbox create python:3.11-slim --network-deny 0.0.0.0/0
```

And the SDK lets you create a sandbox with `network_access=False` for untrusted code. [[3]](https://docs.primeintellect.ai/sandboxes/cli)[[12]](https://docs.primeintellect.ai/sandboxes/sdk)

But note the framing in the docs: the sandbox is **external** — "use an external sandbox or restricted execution environment when the workspace or generated code is untrusted" [[2]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/rlm-runtime.md). It's a *separate tool you reach for*, not a boundary built into the harness. The harness itself runs bare.

So the honest summary: **Prime Agent's local harness has zero containment.** Full user permissions, full network, auto-installing packages, arbitrary subprocess. The "security" story is "review the source of third-party packages before installing" [[6]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/refs/heads/main/packages/coding-agent/README.md) — a human-trust model, not an architectural one.

---

## Bonus: the "IPython kernel" is already dead

This is important for your architecture and it came up cleanly in the search. Prime Agent has **already ripped out IPython and ZMQ.** Two PRs in sequence:

- PR #1686: default switched to a **minimal CPython REPL** (`python -m rlm.repl`) speaking **JSON-lines over stdio** — no ZMQ, no HMAC, no connection files. The Jupyter path remained behind `PRIME_AGENT_KERNEL=ipython`. [[10]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/pull/1686)
- PR #1687: **removed IPython, ZMQ, and cell magics entirely.** `%%bash`, `%cd`, `%env`, and `!` are gone — the model uses `bash()`, `os.chdir`, `os.environ` instead. [[17]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/pull/1687)

So when I earlier said "IPython kernel = a daemon speaking ZMQ," that was *already becoming obsolete* even as we talked. The current Prime Agent is a **bare CPython REPL over stdio** — which is a lot closer to "just an embedded interpreter" than the name implies. Your instinct was right from the start: **it's just an interpreter, and they've been slimming it down to exactly that.**

This matters because it *weakens the kernel-as-daemon mystique* — and it means your C-core replacement isn't competing with a sophisticated Jupyter daemon. It's competing with `python -m rlm.repl` over stdio. The "heavy process" I warned about is real, but the protocol complexity is not what it used to be.

---

## What this resolves for you

1. **Package regulation:** there is none to copy. Prime Agent gives you the *negative example* — full access, auto-install, trust-the-source. Your compute/side-effect split isn't "like Prime Agent but safer"; it's *the thing Prime Agent explicitly refused to build*, and their own docs tell you to go build it externally. You're building it *in* the host, which is the strictly better version of what they outsourced to `prime sandbox`.

2. **Interpreter choice:** the fact they migrated *off* IPython onto a minimal REPL is empirical evidence for your "just need an interpreter" position. They shed the notebook/ZMQ magic because it wasn't load-bearing. The model-facing surface keeps shrinking toward "a Python process you can run code in."

3. **Your C host is the sandbox they're missing.** Every risky capability — network, subprocess, package install, filesystem writes outside the workspace — that Prime Agent hands the kernel *by default*, you gate behind the host. You're not reinventing them; you're completing the half they left out.

Want me to now spec the exact sandbox fence for your C host — the concrete blocklist (network, subprocess, `os`/`socket`/`ctypes`, fork, unrestricted FS writes) and the one escape-hatch path (host-approved side-effect requests) — so the "compute in, side effects out" boundary becomes buildable?

Prime Agent gives each agent session a persistent IPython kernel and a native recursive sub-agent interface. The Python `rlm` package is a model-facing shim; the TypeScript host owns child execution, persistence, usage accounting, and lifecycle.
...
| Component | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `src/core/kernel/index.ts` | ZeroMQ sockets, Jupyter framing, execution, comm dispatch, interrupt, and shutdown. |
| ... src/core/tools/ipython.ts` | Agent tool wrapper ... lazy kernel provisioning, namespace bootstrap, and output shaping. |
...
core/agent-session.ts ... child creation, registry, usage attribution ... cancellation, and goal handlers. |
| `src/core/ ... m-runtime.ts` ... spawn-handle validation ... `rlm ... list, and delete ... |
| ... agent-runtime/src/ ... session-backed harness state. |
...
The kernel is created lazily on first IPython use. Python resolution is:
...
_AGENT_KERNEL ... ipykernel`;
...
/agent/kernel-venv ... uv`; or
...
XDG data ... ~/.prime ... not writable.
...
Startup creates a temporary Jupyter connection file with loopback TCP ports and an HMAC key, starts `python -m ipykernel_launcher`, connects shell, IOPub, and control sockets, waits for subscription propagation, and probes readiness with `kernel_info_request`.

The manager owns the child process, connection directory, ZeroMQ sockets, and a bounded stderr tail. Shutdown sends `shutdown_request`, closes sockets, terminates the process as a fallback, and removes temporary connection data. Persistent sessions may snapshot the kernel namespace into their session artifact directory for revival.
...
IPython processes shell messages serially. Sending the admission response on the shell channel would deadlock: the active `execute_request` cannot finish until the response arrives, while the kernel will not process that shell response until the request finishes.

The Python shim therefore registers comm handlers on the control channel, and the host sends admission responses there. Future completion is scheduled with `loop.call_soon_threadsafe()` because the control handler may run on another thread. Child answers do not use this response path; they arrive later through explicit `agent_message` replies or files.

# Sandbox CLI Guide
...
```bash
prime sandbox create python:3.11-slim \
  --name analytics-lab \
  --cpu-cores 2 \
  --memory-gb 4 \
  --disk-size-gb 20 \
  --timeout-minutes 240 \
  --env PROFILE=production \
  --secret DB_PASSWORD=hunter2
...
Pass a start command after `--` to run your own process when the sandbox boots. There is no shell, so every argument must be its own token:
...
1-slim
...
## Network Isolation

Sandboxes can restrict outbound traffic at creation time. Use an allowlist or a denylist.

```bash
# Deny all egress, including DNS
prime sandbox create python:3.11-slim --network-deny 0.0.0.0/0

# Allow only specific destinations
prime sandbox create python:3.11-slim --network-allow api.openai.com

# Deny specific destinations, allow everything else
prime sandbox create python:3.11-slim --network-deny evil.example.com

```

Both flags are repeatable and accept domains (`example.com`, `*.example.com`) or IPv4 addresses/CIDRs; IPv6 is not supported. Update the rules on a running sandbox with `prime sandbox network --allow ... / --deny ...`.

Network isolation is not available on container sandboxes, which always have full outbound access.
...
## Expose Ports

Make services running inside your sandbox accessible from the internet. Both HTTP and TCP protocols are supported.

Ports must be in the range 22–9000. Ports 8080, 2222, and 8081 cannot be exposed.
...
Expose an HTTP service and get a public HTTPS URL:

```bash
prime sandbox create python:3.11-slim --container --name web-server
# Returns sandbox ID, e.g. sbx_abc123

prime sandbox run <sandbox-id> "nohup python -m http.server 8000 --bind 0.0.0.0 > /dev/null 2>&1 &"

prime sandbox expose <sandbox-id> 8000 --name web-server

prime sandbox list-ports <sandbox-id>

prime sandbox unexpose <sandbox-id> <exposure-id> --yes
...
Expose a raw TCP service and get a public `host:port` endpoint:

```bash
prime sandbox expose <sandbox-id> 9000 --name tcp-server --protocol TCP
...
TCP exposures return an `external_endpoint` (host:port) and `external_port` instead of a URL. Connect using any TCP client.

Use `prime sandbox list-ports ` to see both HTTP and TCP exposures along with their protocols and external ports.
...
Connect to a running sandbox with an interactive shell:
...
The CLI generates an ephemeral key pair, creates a session, and connects automatically. The session is cleaned up on disconnect.

By default, the best available shell is auto-detected (bash > zsh > sh). To use a specific shell:
...
You can also forward ports through the SSH connection:

```bash
prime sandbox ssh <sandbox-id> -- -L 3000:localhost:3000

## Summary 
 
This PR makes Windows a first-class, fully supported runtime for `prime-agent` and fixes fundamental Windows `asyncio` subprocess constraints inside the IPython kernel. 
 
Previously, running Prime Agent on a native Windows environment failed to reach a stable session due to compounding platform assumptions (venv script path resolution, zip extraction stream hangs, flashing console windows, fsync/rename EPERM errors, and ipykernel subprocess limitations). 
 
With these changes, Prime Agent bootstraps cleanly, provisions binaries reliably without flashing console windows, and allows kernel code to spawn subprocesses (e.g. Playwright, Cargo, external CLI tools) and isolate its python environment. 
 
--- 
 
## Key Changes 
 
### 1. Kernel Subprocess & Venv Isolation (`packages/coding-agent/src/core/kernel/index.ts`) 
- **Asyncio Subprocess Fix**: On Windows, `ipykernel` defaults to `WindowsSelectorEventLoopPolicy` (required for `pyzmq`). However, `SelectorEventLoop` cannot spawn subprocesses, causing `asyncio.create_subprocess_exec` (and tools like Playwright or Cargo) to fail with `NotImplementedError`. 
 - *Fix*: Kernel startup re-binds the kernel's existing selector loop to the main thread (keeping `ipykernel` happy) and resets the default event loop policy back to `WindowsProactorEventLoopPolicy`. All worker loops created afterward can spawn subprocesses.
...

...
### 2. Windows Runtime & Bootstrap

context_docs.semantic_identifier: Run the kernel on the REPL runtime
context_docs.blurb:
The TypeScript host now runs the kernel on the REPL runtime by default: `ReplKernelManager` speaks the stdio JSON-lines protocol (no ZMQ, no HMAC, no connection files). The Jupyter path stays present behind `PRIME_AGENT_KERNEL=ipython` and is removed in the next PR.
...
> [!NOTE]
> **High Risk**
> This replaces the default Python execution path and touches kernel lifecycle, persistence, host bridge, and child-process cleanup; regressions would affect every session using the ipython tool.
> 
> **Overview**
> **The coding-agent host now defaults to a minimal CPython REPL kernel** (`python -m rlm.repl`) instead of Jupyter/ipykernel. `ReplKernelManager` drives execution, interrupts, graceful shutdown, snapshot/restore, and typed host requests over **JSON lines on stdio**; the existing ZMQ `KernelManager` remains available when `PRIME_AGENT_KERNEL=ipython`.
> 
> Shared kernel types, MIME parsing, and process signal handling move into `shared.ts`, with a common `KernelClient` surface so the ipython tool provisioner can swap implementations. Bootstrap skips `ipykernel` for the REPL path and extends the runtime readiness probe for REPL protocol v2 (`rlm.emit`, `rlm.repl`).
> 
> ... User-facing notebook behavior ... IPython- ... `%env` listings). ... skills (`agent_message`, `edit`, `attach_image`) emit host display payloads through ... IPython.display`. Tool output can include **unattributed background stdout ... separately from the active cell’s streams.
...
> ### Add `ReplKernelManager` to run the Python kernel on the REPL runtime
> - Introduces `ReplKernelManager` in repl-manager.ts, a JSON-lines stdio client for `python -m rlm.repl` that handles kernel lifecycle, execution, snapshot/restore, host requests, and orphan-process journaling
> - Bumps the REPL protocol to version 2 in repl.py, adding `host_request`/`host_reply` bridging, `list_names`, `rlm.emit`, and prompt failure of pending host requests on shutdown or stdin EOF
> - Rewrites `%%bash`, `%cd`, and `%env` cell magics into equivalent Python in ipython-cell-code.ts so the REPL kernel supports IPython ... like cell semantics
> - Switches skill display helpers in `agent_message`, `edit`, and `attach_image` from `IPython.display.display` to `rlm.emit`, and makes `IpythonKernelProvisioner` select between Jupyter and REPL kernels via `usesIpythonKernel()`
...
> - Risk: `ensureKernelPythonUncached` in bootstrap.ts no longer requires `ipykernel` when `PRIME_AGENT_KERNEL_PYTHON` is set and the REPL client is in use; reviewers should verify that Jupyter-client code paths still enforce the `ipykernel` check via `usesIpythonKernel()`

## Expose Ports

Make services inside your sandbox accessible over the internet. Both HTTP and TCP protocols are supported.

Ports must be in the range 22–9000. Ports 8080, 2222, and 8081 cannot be exposed.
...
By default, sandboxes run `tail -f /dev/null` to keep the container alive for interactive use. Pass `start_command` to override the image's `ENTRYPOINT` with your own process:
...
start_command
...
## Network Isolation

For running untrusted code, create sandboxes without internet access:

```python
async def isolated_sandbox() -> None:
    async with AsyncSandboxClient() as sandboxes:
        # Create a sandbox without outbound internet access
        request = CreateSandboxRequest(
            name="isolated-runner",
            docker_image="python:3.11-slim",
            network_access=False,  # Disable outbound internet
        )
        sandbox = await sandboxes.create(request)
        await sandboxes.wait_for_creation(sandbox.id)

        # Code runs in isolation - no external network calls possible
        result = await sandboxes.execute_command(
            sandbox.id,
            "python -c 'import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen(\"https://example.com\")'",
        )
        # This will fail with a network error

        await sandboxes.delete(sandbox.id)
...
When `network_access=False`:

- Outbound connections to the internet are blocked
- DNS resolution for internal services still works

By default, `network_access=True` and sandboxes have full internet access.

The kernel retains Python state across turns and acts as a control environment for file operations, project commands, installed Python skills, MCP-backed skills, and recursive subagents. The TypeScript host remains responsible for provider calls, session state, tool execution, scheduling, and child-agent lifecycles.

> **Security:** Prime Agent packages run with full system access. Extensions execute arbitrary code, and skills can instruct the model to perform any action including running executables. Review source code before installing third-party packages.

```bash
prime-agent package install npm:@foo/bar@1.0.0
prime-agent package install git:github.com/user/repo@v1
prime-agent package install https://github.com/user/repo  # raw URLs work too
prime-agent package install /absolute/path/to/package
prime-agent package install ./relative/path/to/package
...
By default, `package install` and `package remove` write to global settings (`~/.prime/agent/settings.json`). Use `--local` to write to project settings (`.prime/agent/settings.json`) instead. Project settings can be shared with your team, and Prime Agent installs any missing packages automatically on startup.
...
and `prime-agent package install
...
- Versioned specs are pinned and skipped by `prime-agent package update`.
- Global installs use `npm install -g`.
- Project installs go under `.prime/agent/npm/`.
- Set `npmCommand` in `settings.json` to pin npm package lookup and install operations to a specific wrapper command such as `mise` or `asdf`.
...
- Without `git:` prefix, only protocol URLs are accepted (`https://`, `http://`, `ssh://`, `git://`).
- With `git:` prefix, shorthand formats are accepted, including `github.com/user/repo` and `git@github.com:user/repo`.
- HTTPS and SSH URLs are both supported.
- SSH URLs use your configured SSH keys automatically (respects `~/.ssh/config`).
- For non-interactive runs (for example CI), you can set `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` to disable credential prompts and set `GIT_SSH_COMMAND` (for example `ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=5`) to fail fast.
- Refs pin the package and skip `prime-agent package update`.
- Cloned to `~/.prime/agent/git/ / ` (global) or `.prime/agent/git/ / ` (project).
- Runs `npm install` after clone or pull if `package.json` exists.
...
Third party runtime dependencies belong in `dependencies` in `package.json`. Dependencies that do not register extensions, skills, prompt templates, or themes also belong in `dependencies`. When Prime Agent installs a package from npm or git, it runs `npm install`, so those dependencies are installed automatically.
...
Other resource packages must be bundled in your tarball. Add them to `dependencies` and `bundledDependencies`, then reference their resources through `node_modules/` paths. Prime Agent loads packages with separate module roots, so separate installs do not collide or share modules.
