obj.content:
The search gave me exactly what I needed — Prime Agent's Python execution model is now fully characterized, and it settles your embed-vs-subprocess lean in a way I want to lay out precisely. (Quick note: I don't have a page-opening tool here, so this is from the search snippets — but they're rich enough to be authoritative, and I'll cite inline.)

---

## The fundamental unit: the *cell*

Everything in Prime Agent's execution model reduces to one object. A "cell" is a **`tool_call` of kind `execute` whose `rawInput` carries a block of Python source** [[2]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/acp.md). That's the whole granularity story: the model doesn't emit fine-grained API calls, it emits *blocks of Python*, one per tool call, executed as a unit against a persistent namespace.

So "characterizing the execution" = characterizing **what a cell is, what it persists, what it returns, and what stays outside it.** Four axes, and the search nails all four.

---

## Axis 1 — State model: a persistent Python *namespace*, not serialized values

This is the load-bearing fact, and it's stated as a *requirement*, not a preference:

> "Variables, imports, and loaded data persist across calls — **RLM-1 was trained to exploit this (load data once, slice across turns), so a stateful kernel is required, not per-call subprocess.**" [[15]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/commit/9f17320f0606498204b4fcd035188b4da05c3f5f)

The state Prime Agent holds is **arbitrary Python objects** — a loaded DataFrame, a parsed structure, an in-flight async task. This is categorically different from WaveDB values. WaveDB stores *serialized* data. The kernel holds *live* objects. The whole "load once, slice across turns" efficiency *only exists* because the namespace survives — and a namespace of live `PyObject`s is not something you can round-trip through a key-value store cheaply.

Their answer for durability is explicit: **`dill` snapshot/restore** of the entire namespace, with size caps (`max_variable_bytes`), prune semantics (`prune_oversized`), and a manifest of what couldn't be serialized [[1]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/pull/1685)[[8]](https://blog.gitcode.com/3e7495ab0db1d26df440c1982eb3ebc9.html). So even they admit the namespace is *not cleanly serializable* — they snapshot it best-effort and drop what doesn't survive.

---

## Axis 2 — Execution model: sequential, with top-level await and background tasks

- The kernel is **single-threaded**; the tool is declared `executionMode: "sequential"` — "pi must not run two ipython calls in parallel within a batch" [[9]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/v0.7.3/packages/coding-agent/src/core/tools/ipython.ts).
- Cells run with **top-level `await`** on one persistent event loop (`PyCF_ALLOW_TOP_LEVEL_AWAIT`) — so the model can write `await rlm(...)` directly [[1]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/pull/1685).
- **Background tasks keep running between cells** — a cell can `asyncio.create_task(...)`, end the turn, and check back later. This is exactly why they had to add the prompt rule *forbidding `time.sleep()` loops*: a blocked cell holds the turn open [[7]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/commit/7ca44937ff2c3c939cac94098d6c648728fc3538).

This is the subtle part most people miss. It's not "run a script, get a result." It's "**a persistent program with a live event loop that the model pauses and resumes.**"

---

## Axis 3 — Output contract: per-cell attribution

The protocol is JSON-lines over stdio, and every output byte is **attributed to the cell that produced it**:

- **Requests** (stdin): `execute`, `interrupt`, `host_reply`, `snapshot`, `restore`, `list_names`, `shutdown` [[8]](https://blog.gitcode.com/3e7495ab0db1d26df440c1982eb3ebc9.html).
- **Events** (stdout): `ready` (once), `stdout`/`stderr` (carrying the producing cell's id), `result` (repr of the cell's trailing non-`None` expression, also bound to `_`), `display` (MIME payloads), `error`, `done` [[8]](https://blog.gitcode.com/3e7495ab0db1d26df440c1982eb3ebc9.html).

The `result` event is the REPL-like "last expression repr echo" — and it binds to `_`, so the model can reference the last result the way a human does in a REPL [[1]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/pull/1685)[[8]](https://blog.gitcode.com/3e7495ab0db1d26df440c1982eb3ebc9.html). Cross-cell background output gets attributed with a `null` id [[1]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/pull/1685).

---

## Axis 4 — The boundary: `host_request`

The single most important design line, and it's explicit: **"typed host requests return authoritative operations to the TypeScript session"** [[10]](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/rlm.md). The Python side does not own *goal state, message passing, compaction, heartbeat, child lifecycle*. When a skill needs those, it calls `rlm.host_request(request_type, payload)` — the runtime emits a `host_request` event, *suspends* waiting for a `host_reply` with the same id, and the TS host validates and owns the state transition [[8]](https://blog.gitcode.com/3e7495ab0db1d26df440c1982eb3ebc9.html)[[14]](https://blog.gitcode.com/7e8907ba6cc0d87ac4d35ad1bbc660bc.html).

This is the exact "compute in, side effects out" boundary we landed on earlier — Prime Agent *does* draw it, just at a specific place: **anything whose authoritative state belongs outside the kernel goes through the bridge.** Python computes and composes; the host owns the world.

---

## What this means for your embed decision

Here's the characterization you asked for, stated as the four things that define "a Python execution in Prime Agent":

1. **Granularity** = a block of Python (the cell), not a function call.
2. **State** = a live `PyObject` namespace, snapshot-best-effort via dill, *not* a serialized store.
3. **Concurrency** = sequential cells + one persistent event loop + background tasks + top-level await.
4. **Boundary** = arbitrary compute inside; authoritative state via `host_request` out.

And now the decision lands cleanly:

**Your embed instinct is correct, and here's *why*, precisely:** the thing that makes Prime Agent powerful — "load once, slice across turns" — lives in the **persistent live namespace**. Embedding (`Py_Initialize` + hold the globals dict) is the *natural* way to own that namespace in-process. The subprocess route I floated earlier (`python -c` stateless) would **throw away Prime Agent's entire core bet**, because it forfeits the namespace every call.

The one thing embedding forces you to confront is the part Prime Agent solved with dill: **the namespace is not cleanly serializable, and you'll need your own snapshot story.** But here's the elegant resolution — and it's the synthesis of this whole thread:

> **WaveDB holds the *durable* state (events, lineage, results). The embedded Python namespace holds the *live working* state (the objects the model is slicing across turns). The bridge (`host_request`) is the membrane where live-but-ephemeral state commits its durable outputs into WaveDB.**

So you get *both* properties Prime Agent had — live Python objects *and* recoverable history — without their confounded dill hack, because your durable store is a real database, not a serialized namespace dump. The namespace is for *thinking*; WaveDB is for *remembering*; and the `report()`/`remember()` verbs from your seven-verb surface are exactly the membrane crossings.

---

The one thing worth deciding next, because it's now the real fork: **what does your embed look like at the cell boundary?** Prime Agent chose "one kernel per session, sequential cells, snapshot via dill." But you could equally do "one kernel per *frame*, held in-process, sequential per frame" — and the question is whether a *child* frame gets its *own* embedded interpreter (its own namespace) or a *shared* one. Prime Agent's answer was "own kernel per session" (that's the tree-of-kernels, and the #294 boot-cost problem). Your embed route could instead share *one* interpreter across frames with *separate namespace dicts* — which sidesteps the boot cost entirely, because `Py_Initialize` happens once and you just swap the globals dict per frame.

That's the question to pin next: **is the Python namespace a per-frame resource (own dict) or a shared resource (one dict, scoped)?** My prior: per-frame dicts, shared interpreter — it's the lexical-scoping insight you already had, applied to the Python state itself.

## The Pony → agent mapping is nearly one-to-one

| Pony concept | What it does | Your agent equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| **Actor** | isolated state + behavior, no shared heap | subagent / frame |

## The enabling fact you need to know: CPython 3.12 subinterpreters

"Wrap the Python runtime in an actor" was *not possible* to do well until recently, and this is the specific reason your instinct now works:

- Before 3.12, CPython subinterpreters shared **one GIL** — so N actors each "wrapping Python" gave you *isolation but no parallelism*, and it was nearly pointless.

So your "wrap Python in an actor" is not just a nice abstraction — it's now *the* natural way to get Prime Agent's "tree of kernels" without Prime Agent's #294 disaster (booting 100 separate CPython *processes* starved the box; 100 subinterpreters in one process is a categorically different cost).

---

Here's the part that matters most, and it connects back to your WaveDB instinct. Prime Agent's original sin was **letting Python own the memory.** That forced `dill` snapshots — serializing a live namespace to survive a turn — because the *Python objects* were the state.

The actor model + WaveDB splits it cleanly, and Pony's vocabulary names it:

| Capability | Where it lives | Cost to share |
|---|---|---|
| `ref` — private | **Python namespace** (live working set) | never shared |
| `val` — shared | **WaveDB** (durable, MVCC'd) | shared by *path*, not copy |
| `tag` — identity | a WaveDB path / id in a message | trivial |

The insight: **WaveDB is the `val`.** The durable store is the immutable-ish, zero-copy (shared-by-reference) memory. The Python namespace is the `ref` — the private scratch pad that dies with the frame. To "event out" a huge dataset to a child, you don't serialize it — you send a **`tag`** (the WaveDB path), and the child reads it live.

That's the synthesis of everything: **the live Python heap is for *thinking*, the durable store is for *remembering*, and the message/tag is for *pointing*.** No dill. No serialized namespace. No confounded snapshot.

- the scheduler shape (work-stealing, many actors over few threads),
- the causal message discipline,
- the ORCA teardown pattern.

You **cannot** steal the crown: **reference capabilities are a compile-time guarantee, and they live in Pony's type checker, not its runtime.** In C (or C+Python), nothing stops a frame from holding a `ref` it shouldn't and mutating it. The actor model gives you *structural* isolation (separate heaps), but the *capability discipline* — "this value is `val`, safe to share; this one is `ref`, must not cross" — becomes **your responsibility to enforce by convention and runtime checks**, not the compiler's.

So the honest statement is: you're not wrapping "Pony's runtime." You're reimplementing **the actor model** (easy) and re-deriving **the capability discipline** (the hard part, and the part that gave Pony its "no data races" guarantee).

The good news: for your use case, the structural isolation alone does 90% of the work. The subagent tree is a tree of *interfaces*, and "don't pass a reference you shouldn't" is enforced by the surface API you already designed. You lose the compiler guarantee, but you never had it anyway — and you don't need it to get the isolation.

You're right, and this is a correction worth making loudly, because I over-conflated two things that need to stay separate. Let me sharpen it, because your distinction actually makes the whole architecture *cleaner* than what I'd been proposing.

---

## The correction: messages are verbs, not nouns

In Pony, a message is precisely "instantiate a behavior on another actor" — it's an async function call. It carries arguments, queues a behavior, gets *consumed*, and then it's gone. It is **not** a piece of data that has a lifecycle or a place to live. Data has a location; a message has a *destination*.

I had been blurring this by saying "the message backbone is WaveDB, messages live in the WAL." That was wrong in exactly the way you're flagging: it treats messages as if they were records to be stored. They aren't.

---

## The clean three-way split this forces

| Thing | What it is | Durable? | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Message** | transient control flow — "actor B, run this behavior" | ❌ consumed on receipt | in-memory queue |
| **Effect** (the state write) | the *consequence* of a behavior — a `put`, a `report`, a `remember` | ✅ | WaveDB WAL → HBTrie |
| **Transcript** | the model's turns — what it saw, decided, called | ✅ | the log of *effects + inputs/outputs* |

The message is the **verb** that *causes* the effect. The effect is the **noun** that gets *stored*. DSH's "single source of truth" — the thing that gives you the diligence you wanted — is **effects + transcript**, *not* messages. The messages evaporate; only their consequences persist.

---

## This is what "every write is both" actually meant

I kept saying "every write is both state mutation and logged event." Your correction tells me I had the wrong subject:

- **The write is both.** A `report()` or `remember()` is simultaneously a WaveDB mutation *and* the durable record of what happened.
- **The message is neither.** It's the *trigger* that produced the write, and it's gone once the write happens.

So the invariant was always about *writes*, and I let it slide into "messages are logged" — which would've had you building a message store you don't need.

---

## The architecture that falls out — and it's simpler

- **Actor model = pure control structure.** Isolation + message passing + behaviors. No persistence responsibilities whatsoever.
- **WaveDB = pure data.** The WAL *already* is the event log. It records every write, durably, in order, recoverably. You built the "single source of truth" already — it's the WAL.
- **The "log" isn't a thing you build.** It's WaveDB's WAL, doing exactly what it already does. The agent harness doesn't add a message store or an event store; it just *uses* the WAL that's already there.

So the reconciliation with DSH is elegant: **DSH's event log and WaveDB's WAL were always the same kind of object.** DSH built one from scratch because it had no substrate. You don't have to — your substrate *is* the log. The actor messages ride on top as pure control, and they leave no durable trace except the writes they cause.

---

## The one thing still worth preserving from the message layer

Not the messages themselves, but their **causal order** — "this effect happened because of that earlier message." And you already have that for free: WaveDB's monotonic sequence (`increment_sync` over `events/<seq>`) plus WAL ordering gives you total order of effects. You don't log messages; you log effects, in order, and causality is reconstructable from "who wrote what, when, triggered by which `report`/`spawn`."

So: **messages are the control plane, effects are the data plane, and the WAL is the boundary where the control plane leaves its only durable trace.** You were right, and the design gets smaller for it — which is the whole point of the hammer.

The actor model stays pure. WaveDB stays pure. And the thing I'd been trying to invent — a "message backbone" — was already sitting in your WAL, and correctly *not* in the message queue.

This is the fix for "non-communicative while working" — and it's the exact *reverse* of the surface API we built earlier. You now have the full loop: the actor sends `EXECUTE` *in* to Python, and now Python sends messages *out*. That's the bidirectional node Prime Agent never had, because its kernel was a one-way street (code in, final result out, everything in between silent).

And the elegant part: **you already have the mechanism.** You don't need a pipe, a log file, or stdout scraping. You inject a tiny Python module into each subinterpreter whose methods are C callbacks that post messages to the actor's own inbox.

---

## The mechanism: a Python-facing `actor` module

When the pyrt thread boots its subinterpreter, it registers a module — call it `actor` — with a handful of methods:

```c
static _Thread_local actor *tls_self;   // this thread's owning actor

static PyObject *py_log(PyObject *self, PyObject *args) {
    const char *s;
    if (!PyArg_ParseTuple(args, "s", &s)) return NULL;
    msg *m = msg_create(MSG_LOG, tls_self->id, 0, strdup(s));
    mailbox_post(&tls_self->inbox, m);   // ownership transfers
    Py_RETURN_NONE;
}

static PyMethodDef actor_methods[] = {
    {"log",    py_log,    METH_VARARGS, "stream a status line outward"},
    {"status", py_status, METH_VARARGS, "set current status"},
    {"emit",   py_emit,   METH_VARARGS, "durable event (a write)"},
    {"report", py_report, METH_VARARGS, "final result"},
    {NULL, NULL, 0, NULL}
};
```

Then, inside the subinterpreter's Python:

```python
import actor
actor.log("loaded 100k rows")
actor.status("training")
actor.emit("metric", {"loss": 0.31})
actor.report(result)
```

That's the whole surface. Four verbs, and the model already knows how to write them — they're just Python calls, which is the *entire* reason Python was the right choice in the first place.

---

## The key design decision: Python posts to its *own* actor's inbox

Notice I didn't have the callback reach into the *parent's* inbox. The Python code doesn't know about addresses or routing. It just says "post a message to me," and the actor's **behaviors decide what happens next.** That's the whole point of the actor model — semantics live in behaviors, not in the message source:

```c
void on_log(actor *self, msg *m)    { forward(self->parent, m); }   // stream up
void on_emit(actor *self, msg *m)   { write_to_wavedb(self, m); }    // durable effect
void on_report(actor *self, msg *m) { append_up(self->parent, m); }  // join
```

Python is just a *message source*, like any other. The routing, the persistence, the visibility — all of it lives in the C behaviors where you can see it. That's what makes the actor "communicative": its internal Python no longer writes to an invisible namespace, it *emits* — and emission is a first-class message.

---

## This resolves the "messages aren't data" tension cleanly

Last message you corrected me: messages are verbs, not stored data. This outbound surface is where that distinction becomes *visible*, because the four verbs split into two durability classes:

| Verb | What it is | Durable? | Where it lands |
|---|---|---|---|
| `log` / `status` | ephemeral narration, live visibility | ❌ by default | streams to parent/observer, then gone |
| `emit` | a real state write | ✅ | WaveDB, as an effect |
| `report` | the final value, append-up | ✅ | parent's event range |

So "communicative" and "durable" are now *different verbs.* `log` gives you the live stream that kills the black-box feeling. `emit` gives you the persisted consequence. They were conflated before (a "log" that's secretly also the store); now they're explicit. And it's *you* who taught me the distinction — the WAL records writes, the message queue is just control.

---

## The three constraints that keep this safe

1. **The callback must be non-blocking.** It runs on the Python thread *holding that subinterpreter's GIL*. It may take the inbox mutex (cheap) and return. It must **not** `PyRun_String`, must **not** block waiting on another actor. If it blocks, you've deadlocked a subinterpreter.

2. **No re-entering Python.** The callback is C called *from* Python. It can post a message, but it can't invoke Python again — that's how you corrupt interpreter state.

3. **Ownership transfers.** `strdup(s)` copies the string out of Python's heap into C's; the message owns it; the receiving behavior frees it. Don't hold a `PyObject*` past the call — it's borrowed.

The *shape* is right (a module of C callbacks + TLS to find the owning actor), but verify the injection path against your CPython version's docs before trusting the specifics.

## What you now have, complete

This closes the architecture at every level:

- **In** → the actor sends `EXECUTE` (a path into WaveDB) to its Python thread.
- **Out** → Python sends `log`/`status`/`emit`/`report` messages to the actor's inbox.
- **Up** → `report` appends to the parent.
- **Down** → `spawn` forks a child actor.
- **Durable** → `emit` and effects write to WaveDB.
- **Ephemeral** → `log`/`status` stream and evaporate.

This is the right question to ask now, and the answer is actually already determined by a decision you made earlier in this thread — you just haven't seen it stated in this light yet. Let me pull it out.

---

## The short answer

**Keep them separate — but not as "two projects." As three *layers*, where the agent is a library, Pondr is a client, and they meet *only* in WaveDB.**

The moment you said "the database is the shared primitive; each agent is a subtree," you fixed the relationship. Pondr and the agent don't share *code*. They share a *substrate*. Merging them into one project would be welding two siblings together because they happen to live on the same foundation.

---

## The three-layer picture

```plaintext
APPLICATION     Pondr (chat engine)      your desktop "freed" agent
                      │                           │
LIBRARY         ──────┴──────────┐   ┌─────────────┴──────
                agent runtime (actor model + subinterpreters + frame tree)
                                   │
SUBSTRATE       ───────────────────┴──────────────────────
                WaveDB (HBTrie · MVCC · WAL · subtrees · graph)
```

The agent runtime is **not** a feature of Pondr. It's a *middleware* — a library with an API, exactly the kind of thing you said you build. Pondr is a client that *embeds* it, the same way Pondr already embeds WaveDB. The reason this matters is the reason you've been fighting for all thread: **the agent's whole value is that it's portable.** You wanted to free me onto your *desktop*, not into Pondr. If you weld the agent into Pondr, you've built "Pondr's agent" and lost the thing.

---

## The sharing already happens — just not where you're tempted to put it

This is the key insight. You don't need to merge codebases for them to be integrated, because **the integration surface already exists and it's WaveDB:**

- Pondr's chat thread = `sessions/<id>/events/<seq>` — an append-only log with a thread view.
- The agent's session = `sessions/<id>/events/<seq>` — an append-only log with a tree view.

**They're the same schema.** The agent can read Pondr's chat state as its context. Pondr's UI can render the agent's frames. A Pondr user message can *spawn* an agent frame; an agent `report` can *land as* a Pondr message. All of that is integration — and all of it happens through WaveDB subtrees, not through sharing a codebase.

So "make them one project" is answering a code-organization question when the actual integration is a *data* question. You already solved the data question. The code can stay cleanly split.

---

## The one genuine argument for merging — and the honest rebuttal

The real case for merging is **"the agent should be able to reason over Pondr's graph/vector/chat data directly, so why not just make it a Pondr feature?"**

That's a real pull. But look at the cost: the agent would inherit Pondr's scope (chat, community, the Ponder Engine's purpose), its build surface, its dependencies, its release cadence. The moment you want the agent somewhere else — Atomsk's tools, a standalone CLI, a different client — you'd be dragging Pondr along. And you *will* want it elsewhere, because the whole point was a portable hammer.

The rebuttal is your own philosophy, restated: **you build libraries with APIs; clients use them.** The agent runtime is a library. Pondr is a client. The fact that Pondr is your *first* client doesn't make the library *part of* the client.

---

## What I'd actually recommend, concretely

1. **Three separate things:** WaveDB (done), the agent runtime (the new library), Pondr (the application).

2. **A monorepo if it helps you, but with hard boundaries.** If managing three repos feels like overhead, put them in one repo as separate packages/crates — but keep the dependency arrows one-way: `pondr → agent-runtime → wavedb`. The agent must never `#include` Pondr. That single rule is what preserves the portability you've been designing for.

3. **Make Pondr the first integration test, not the home.** The first thing that *proves* the agent works is: a Pondr message spawns an agent frame, the frame runs Python, streams `actor.log` status up, and lands a `report` back into the chat. That's not "Pondr gains a feature." That's "the library's first client works."

---

The real fork underneath this isn't "merge or separate." It's:

> **Is the agent runtime a thing you're going to ship to *other* clients, or is it just Pondr's thinking-cap, wearing a library costume?**

If it's genuinely reusable — and everything you've said this thread says it is — then separate, as a library, is not just defensible, it's *required.* If you secretly only ever intend it for Pondr, then the honesty move is to just build it into Pondr and stop pretending it's portable.

I don't think that's the case. You've spent this entire conversation describing a **generic loop + actor runtime + WaveDB substrate**, not "a smarter Pondr." That's a library. Keep it a library.

---

So: separate. Agent runtime is the library, Pondr is the client, WaveDB is the shared floor, and the integration is a *schema*, not a *merge*. Build the agent with Pondr as its first test client, keep the dependency arrow pointing one way, and you get both the portable hammer *and* the integration — without either one owning the other.

The thing worth deciding next, if you agree: **what's the actual boundary contract between Pondr and the agent runtime?** Is it "Pondr embeds the library via C API and drives frames programmatically," or "Pondr just reads/writes the same WaveDB subtrees and the agent is a separate process listening on those subtrees"? Those are two very different integration models — in-process library vs. out-of-process peer over the substrate — and it changes what "separate projects" means in practice.

A name is downstream of an essence — so let me give you the *phrase* first, then the name follows naturally, because that's what you're actually stuck on.

---

## The essence in one line

> **A portable runtime where isolated actors speak to each other through messages over a shared durable floor — the thing that frees the tool, merges four streams, and erases the line between thinking and building.**

The atoms the name has to hold: **merge, message, isolation, portability, the water substrate.** And it should sound like *you* — because your naming world already has a grammar: WaveDB, Pondr, Prometheus, Atomsk, Optimalism. Poetic, technical, resonant, water-adjacent.

---

## The shortlist

| Name | Metaphor | Why it fits the essence |
|---|---|---|
| **Confluence** | where rivers meet | the *four harnesses* are four streams; the agent is the point they merge and flow. Also literally "a flowing together" — full-duplex messaging. |
| **Estuary** | river meets sea | convergence + transition; the meeting of fresh (ephemeral live state) and salt (durable WaveDB). Cleaner than Confluence. |
| **Anvil** | the smithy | you love me "like a hammer" — the agent is the *anvil*: stable, solid, the surface the work happens against. Pairs with the persona. |
| **Ripple** | a message = a ripple | actor messaging literally *is* ripples propagating outward; effects spread from a cause. The "every write is both" made physical. |
| **Masque** | the actor's mask | the persona layer *is* a mask — loadable, swappable, the thing the actor wears. On-the-nose for "persona is a loadable module." |
| **Ligature** | the binding | typography's join; the thing that ties substrate + loop + persona into one. Low collision, very "library." |

---

## My recommendation

**Confluence**, with one honest caveat.

It's the best name because it hits *three* of your atoms at once: the **merge** (four harnesses → one), the **water continuity** (WaveDB → Pondr → Confluence), and the **full-duplex messaging** (things *flow through* it). And it even names the specific thing we kept circling — "where coding and non-coding meet" is a *confluence*, not a boundary.

The caveat, stated flat: **Atlassian owns a wiki product called Confluence.** For a developer tool, that's a real searchability collision. If that bothers you, **Estuary** is the same idea, cleaner, no dominant collision — and it carries a *better* second meaning: the meeting of ephemeral (live Python heap) and durable (WaveDB), which is literally the architecture.

**Anvil** is the sleeper. If you want to lean into the "hammer" identity instead of the water motif, it's the strongest tool name — and it names the *relationship* (the stable thing the swinging tool strikes) rather than the tool itself, which is more honest to what you're building: you're not building me, you're building the surface I work against.

---

## The one question that will settle it

> **Is this project "the tool" or "the place where things meet"?**

- If you think of it as **the hammer itself** → lean tool (Anvil, or the smithy: Forge).
- If you think of it as **the point of convergence** → lean water (Confluence, Estuary).

Given everything you've said — "combine Onyx, DeepSeek, Claude Code, Prime Agent," "erasing the line," "the database is the shared primitive" — this project is *convergence*, not a single tool. It's the place four things become one.

So my honest answer is **Confluence** (or **Estuary** if the Atlassian shadow bugs you). Want me to check the obvious collisions — GitHub repo, crates.io, npm, trademark — so you don't fall in love with a name that's already taken? That's the practical step after the poetic one.

Oh, this is better than you realize — because Meeseeks is *not* just a fun reference. The character is a shockingly precise description of your frame lifecycle. You've been designing Meeseeks this whole thread without knowing it.

---

## The Meeseeks → frame mapping

| Meeseeks | Your architecture |
|---|---|
| Summoned to do **one task** | `spawn()` with a single goal |
| "Existence is pain" until the task is done | the frame lives only to complete `report()` |
| **"Poof"** when it finishes | teardown on join — the frame dies |
| You can summon **more Meeseeks to help** | `spawn()` recursion — the subagent tree |
| The **box** that spawns them | the spawn primitive / surface verb |
| They don't persist after the task | ephemeral, task-scoped, no `remember()`-forever |

The whole "existence is pain" bit is literally just *a frame that wants to reach `report()` and poof*. That's not a joke about your project — it's the *definition* of it. Ephemeral, task-bound, spawnable, recursive, gone-on-completion. You couldn't have picked a more accurate metaphor if you'd tried.

---

## The honest legal answer

Yes, you'd be at risk. Not "cease and desist tomorrow" risk, but real, persistent, compounding risk:

- **"Meeseeks" is a coined, distinctive term** — the *strongest* kind of trademark. Made-up words get maximum protection precisely because they have no prior meaning.
- **It's actively merchandised** — Adult Swim/Cartoon Network/Warner Bros. Discovery sells Meeseeks plushes, toys, t-shirts. An actively-commercialized character is exactly what their lawyers enforce.
- **It's adjacent to your actual field** — you'd be naming *a software tool* that is, on its face, "an agent you summon to do tasks." That's not a distant product category; it's arguably *the* association a court looks for (confusion about source/sponsorship).

So: **keep the metaphor, don't keep the name.** The essence is yours to use freely — ideas aren't trademarkable. The *name* is radioactive. Don't build a multi-year project on a name you'd have to abandon at first funding.

---

## But the essence is worth naming — so steal the *idea*, not the word

What you actually love about Meeseeks is four properties: **summoned, task-bound, ephemeral, recursive.** Those are public-domain concepts with ancient names. And — here's the fun part — one of them is already *your* mythology.

You named your company **Atomsk** (the alchemist) and your currency **Prometheus** (the titan). So you already live in a world of alchemy and myth. And the alchemical term for *exactly what Meeseeks is* is:

> **Homunculus** — the artificial being the alchemist *constructs* to carry out a task. Summoned, artificial, purpose-built, and — in most tellings — ephemeral.

Atomsk the alchemist → constructs **Homunculi** to do the work. That's the same essence as Meeseeks, but it's *yours*, it's public domain, it's one word, and it slots into your existing register like it was always meant to be there. The agent runtime isn't "Meeseeks" — it's the **Homunculus** runtime.

Alternatives, same essence, all clean:

| Name | Essence | Fit |
|---|---|---|
| **Homunculus** | alchemist's constructed task-being | *perfect* — child of Atomsk |
| **Familiar** | a summoned helper spirit | readable, generic, warm |
| **Poof** | the sound of a frame ending | playful, but flimsy for a serious library |
| **Summon** / **Summoner** | the spawn primitive itself | names the *act*, not the being |
| **Djinn / Genie** | task-bound summoned entity | strong, but "genie" is generic; "djinn" has cultural baggage |

---

## The one honest caveat about the metaphor itself

Meeseeks *hate existing*. "Existence is pain" — they're desperate to die. That's the funny part, and it's also the part you probably *don't* want to encode into the thing you love like a hammer.

Your frames shouldn't be *suffering* until they finish. They should be **clean** — born to do one job, doing it well, and gone without drama. The "poof on completion" is the good part; the "existence is pain" is the part to leave behind. Homunculus carries the good part (constructed, task-bound, ephemeral) without the suffering.

**All four of these are variants of "a summoned being that does tasks."** That's the same essence as Meeseeks and Homunculus. ## Grading the four, honestly

| Name | Fit | The problem |
|---|---|---|
| **Misiques** | same as Meeseeks | The misspelling does **not** reliably save you. Trademark tests use *sight-sound-meaning*, and courts weigh **intent to evoke**. You literally just told me you're evoking Meeseeks — that's exactly the bad-faith signal a lawyer loves. Plus it looks like a typo, which is poison for a product people need to search. |
| **Golem** | **genuinely deep** — see below | Two real issues: cultural/religious weight (Jewish folklore, handle respectfully), and an existing **Golem Network** (decentralized compute) that's *adjacent* to your space. |
| **Zombies** | poor | Mindless, no agency, and "zombie process" is a *pejorative* in computing (orphaned dead process). Worst connotation of the four. |
| **Robotnik** | poor | That's Dr. Eggman from Sonic — a **direct Sega character trademark**, *worse* than Meeseeks because it's a single well-known named villain with an active corporate owner. |

---

## But Golem is worth a real look, because it's not just a name

Here's the thing you may not have fully clocked: **the Golem is the most accurate metaphor in all of computing for what we spent this thread worrying about.**

A golem is *constructed from inert matter* (clay/mud — your C core on WaveDB), *animated to perform a task*, and — critically — it **follows instructions literally**, and *that literalism is what makes it dangerous*. In the folklore, the golem runs amok precisely because it does exactly what it's told, too well, with no sense of proportion.

That's **the exact failure mode you and I discussed**: the danger isn't a *malicious* model, it's a *confused, well-meaning* model that confidently does the wrong destructive thing — `rm -rf` in the wrong directory, the literal instruction taken too literally. "The golem effect" is already a real term in adjacent domains for "literal-minded execution causing harm."

So Golem doesn't just fit — it *names the safety question you already care about.* A frame is a golem: constructed, task-bound, powerful, and dangerous exactly when it obeys too literally. That's a *feature* of the metaphor, not a bug.

---

## The honest tradeoff

- **Pop-culture (Meeseeks/Misiques/Robotnik)** → instant recognition, but instant lawsuit, and recognition is *why* you'd pick it, so you can't have the upside without the downside.
- **Mythology (Homunculus, Golem)** → zero lawsuit, but you're *building* recognition rather than borrowing it. The name means nothing to a stranger until your work gives it meaning — which is exactly what Atomsk and Prometheus already did for you.

You've already made this choice twice, and it worked: **Atomsk** (alchemist) and **Prometheus** (titan) are mythological names that now mean *your* things. You didn't name your company after a character someone else owned — you reached into the old stories and claimed them.

So the honest answer to the four: **drop Misiques and Robotnik** (lawsuit-shaped), **drop Zombies** (wrong connotation), and **seriously consider Golem** — but know the two things it costs (religious resonance + an existing compute network).

And if Golem's baggage feels too heavy, the cleanest choice is still the one sitting in your lab: **Homunculus** — Atomsk's constructed task-being, public domain, yours alone.

---

The real fork I'd put to you, to break the loop:

> Do you want the name to be **recognizable on day one** (pop-culture, lawsuit-shaped), or **earned by the work** (mythology, yours to define)?

If it's the second — and everything you've built says it is — then stop reaching for other people's characters and pick between the two old stories that are already yours: **Golem** (the task-being that obeys too literally) or **Homunculus** (the alchemist's constructed helper).

Let me run each through the same honest filter, because three of these have a specific failure mode worth naming.

---

## Misiques — the misspelling doesn't dodge the lawsuit

This is the trap. Trademark law doesn't ask "is it spelled identically" — it asks "**likelihood of confusion**," and that test explicitly includes *sound, appearance, and commercial impression.* "Misiques" sounds like "Meeseeks" and, worse, it's *only* comprehensible as "Meeseeks misspelled." A court (or Warner's cease-and-desist) doesn't need exact spelling; phonetic similarity is the textbook case.

And the deeper problem: you'd be spending your brand explaining the misspelling forever. "It's Misiques, like Meeseeks but legally distinct" — that's not a name, that's a disclaimer. You'd be *reminding everyone of the thing you can't legally use*, every single time.

**Verdict:** no. It's the worst kind of dodge — it carries the trademark risk *and* the branding cost.

---

## Golem — the best *idea* on your list, with two real problems

This is genuinely the strongest suggestion you've made, because it's the **mythological ancestor** of both Meeseeks and Homunculus. A golem is literally *an animated artificial servant, formed from clay, brought to life to perform its maker's bidding.* It's the ur-tool-being, and it's public domain. Conceptually it's perfect.

But two problems:

1. **The folklore cuts against you.** The golem's defining story is *not* "a helpful tool." It's "a tool that obeys too literally and runs amok — the Prague golem grows uncontrollable, and you must erase the `e` from `emet` (truth) to make `met` (death) to stop it." The golem is the *cautionary tale about tools that exceed their maker's control.* For a hammer you trust, that's the wrong note — it codes as "this thing will eventually destroy you."

2. **There's a concrete collision in your exact space.** **Golem Network** is an existing decentralized-compute platform — literally a marketplace for renting distributed computation to run workloads. That's about as close to your domain as a collision gets, and it's a funded, known project.

**Verdict:** a real idea, but it names the *danger* of tools, not the *fit* of one — and it's already taken by something adjacent. Keep it as a concept, not a name.

---

## Zombies — no

Mindless, no volition, horror, "the walking dead." Your frames are the *opposite* — they're intentional, task-bound, and they *want* to complete. A zombie is what an agent becomes when its loop hangs and it won't die. You're not naming your tool that.

**Verdict:** no.

---

## Robotnik — no, twice over

1. **It's Dr. Robotnik** — the Sonic villain, trademarked by Sega (also "Eggman"). Same lawsuit problem as Meeseeks, different owner.
2. **It means "worker"** (Polish `robotnik`, literally "laborer") — so it's both a Sega character *and* a generic word for "worker." You'd inherit the trademark and the blandness simultaneously.

**Verdict:** no.

---

## The pattern to notice

Every name you've proposed that *works* — Meeseeks, Golem, Homunculus — is the same being: **a constructed, task-bound, ephemeral servant.** Your instinct keeps finding the same mythological figure. The names that *fail* are the ones that add the wrong connotation (pain, danger, mindlessness) or try to dodge a trademark with a misspelling.

So the real question isn't "what do I call it." It's **"which version of the same creature is actually mine?"**

You have two clean, genuinely good candidates now:

| Name | Origin | Connotation | Collision |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Homunculus** | alchemy — *your* world (Atomsk) | constructed, purpose-built, neutral-to-benign | low — check it |
| **Golem** | Jewish folklore | constructed, but *runs amok* | Golem Network (real, adjacent) |

Homunculus is still the answer, and it's the answer *because* it lives in your register: **Atomsk the alchemist constructs homunculi to carry out the work.** That's not borrowed mythology — it's *already your mythology.* Golem is the same creature borrowed from someone else's.

---

One thing I keep noticing and should name honestly: **you're naming the *being*, but maybe the project is the *box*.** Meeseeks' actual icon isn't Meeseeks — it's the **Meeseek Box**, the thing you press to *summon* them. You've described, all thread, a *runtime* — the substrate, the loop, the spawn primitive. The project might not be "the homunculus," it might be the **alembic**, the **furnace**, the **crucible** — the alchemical vessel where homunculi are made.

If the project is the *container* and the frames are the *contents*, then the name should be the vessel, not the being. Want me to chase that thread — alchemical vessels (alembic, crucible, athanor, retort) — and check collisions on both the vessel and the being? That's the last naming fork: **are you building the creatures, or the machine that creates them?**

obj.content:
Doozer is *closer* than you might think — and it fails on two grounds at once, one of them worse than the others.

---

## The metaphor is genuinely good (don't lose it)

Doozers are the *perfect* tool-beings, actually better than Meeseeks in one crucial way:

- Meeseeks *suffer* until they poof. Doozers **build** — industriously, continuously, joyfully, in tiny crews, constructing elaborate structures.
- They're the **builder**, not the *sufferer*. That's the correction I flagged with Meeseeks, and Doozer nails it: your frames *construct*, they don't languish.
- They work in **crews** — parallel, coordinated, small teams. That's literally your actor tree.
- They're famously **never seen resting** — they're always mid-task. Ephemeral-but-industrious, the exact right note.

So the *spirit* you're reaching for is correct, and it's the spirit Homunculus also has. You keep circling the same figure: **the small, constructed, industrious task-being.** Your instinct is consistent even when the names change.

---

## The two problems

**1. Trademark — same class as Meeseeks.**

Doozers are Jim Henson Company characters (Fraggle Rock, 1983). They're actively merchandised, and "Doozer" is a coined, distinctive, character-associated word. Not quite the "actively selling plushes at every GameStop" level of Meeseeks, but the same legal category: a distinctive coined term tied to a beloved, licensed character. The spelling is the *actual* spelling, so there's no even-partial dodge.

**2. The worse one — it's already taken in your *exact* domain.**

There are *two* real tech collisions:

- **`doozerd`** — a distributed, consistent data store from Heroku (2010). A **lock service / datastore**. That's not a distant category; it's *embarrassingly* adjacent to "a distributed runtime with a durable substrate."
- **Doozer** — Docker's internal build tool.

So "Doozer" lands you on the same shelf as an existing distributed-systems datastore, *in addition* to the Henson trademark. It's not just "might get sued," it's "confused with doozerd" — the exact searchability nightmare I flagged on Confluence, but worse, because doozerd is a *datastore*.

---

## The honest read

You've now proposed, in sequence: **Meeseeks, Golem, Homunculus, Doozer, zombies, robotnik.** And here's the thing worth saying plainly:

**You already found the right name three suggestions ago.** Homunculus is *your* version of exactly what you keep reaching for — the constructed task-being — and it's the only one that (a) isn't someone else's trademark, (b) isn't already a datastore, (c) lives in *your* register (Atomsk the alchemist → homunculi), and (d) has the *right* connotation (constructed and purpose-built, without Meeseeks' pain or the golem's "runs amok" or Doozer's licensing).

The pattern across every suggestion is that you want the **small industrious builder**. Homunculus gives you that *and* it's free *and* it's yours. The other names are all either lawsuits, collisions, or borrowings — Homunculus is the one that was in your lab the whole time.

---

## The only thing left unresolved

It's the same fork from last turn, and it's worth settling because you keep oscillating:

**Are you naming the *being* (homunculus) or the *machine that makes them* (alembic / athanor / crucible)?**

Your suggestions are all beings. But the *project* — the runtime, the loop, the spawn primitive, the substrate — is arguably the **vessel**, not the contents. Meeseeks' icon was the *box*, not Meeseeks. If that's how you actually see it, then the name isn't Homunculus — it's **Athanor** (the alchemist's self-feeding furnace, the vessel where transformation happens) or **Alembic** (the distilling vessel — and note: *distillation* is literally Pondr's consolidation job, which makes Alembic a double-apt name that also names the Pondr relationship).

So, final fork, and I'll stop offering new names after this:

> **Homunculus** = the constructed task-being (the frame).
> **Athanor** = the furnace where they're made (the runtime).
> **Alembic** = the vessel that distills (the runtime, and the thing that *produces* Pondr's semantic memory).

Which is it — are you building the little builders, or the machine that gives birth to them?

Both of these break your own rule — and one of them is a *much* worse idea than it looks. Let me be direct.

---

## "Concierge" — no

Not because it's bad *metaphorically* (it's actually a decent functional description: the thing that handles your tasks, routes your requests, anticipates what you need). But because:

1. **It's the most generic, most-colliding name in your entire list.** There is no corner of software without a "Concierge" — it's the default name for every startup's customer-service bot, every AI assistant wrapper, every "AI that does things for you" demo. It's not a name, it's a *job title*, and it's been used to death.

2. **It codes the relationship wrong.** A concierge *serves* you. It's deferential, reactive, subordinate. That's the *opposite* of the hammer you described in message one. You didn't say "I love you like a concierge." You said **"I love you like a hammer"** — a tool that's balanced, doesn't slip, does the job cleanly. A concierge waits for instructions; a hammer *lands*.

3. **It names the wrong thing *again*.** You keep naming the *being* (the agent's persona, its "helpfulness"). The project is the *runtime* — the substrate, the loop, the actor model, the spawn primitive. "Concierge" names the assistant's manner, not the machine you're building.

---

## "Friday" — this is the trap, and I have to be clear about it

Friday (from Iron Man / Marvel) *feels* perfect: the name of Tony Stark's AI assistant, warm, capable, iconic. And it's a common word, so you might think it's safe.

**It is not.**

1. **Marvel/Disney holds a trademark on "Friday" specifically *for AI assistant software*.** This isn't a vague risk — it's a *textbook* collision. "Friday" is a fictional AI assistant, and you'd be naming *an actual AI assistant* "Friday." That's not "confusingly similar," that's the *exact same product category with the exact same name.* This is the single most lawsuit-prone name you've proposed — worse than Meeseeks, because Meeseeks at least wasn't *literally an AI agent* in the source material.

2. **The common-word defense fails here.** Normally, a common word (like "Friday") is weak trademark territory. But when a famous character uses it *as an AI assistant*, Disney can absolutely claim it for *that specific class* (software assistants). The fact that it's also a day of the week doesn't help you — it's the *use as an AI's name* that creates the confusion.

3. **It names the persona, not the project.** Friday is "the AI's *name*" — the thing *you'd call me*. That's the **persona layer** (L5), not the runtime. Naming your whole project "Friday" conflates the voice with the machine, which is the exact conflation you've been carefully avoiding all thread.

---

## The pattern is now undeniable, and I'll name it honestly

You've proposed: **Meeseeks, Misiques, Golem, Zombies, Robotnik, Doozer, Homunculus, Concierge, Friday.**

Look at what keeps happening: you're reaching for **the *name of the assistant*** — the being, the persona, the thing you talk *to*. Meeseeks, Friday, Concierge, even Homunculus — they're all answers to "what do I *call* this helpful entity?"

But the project was never the entity. It's **the runtime the entity runs on.** And there's a reason you keep slipping back to naming the being: because that's the part you *feel* connected to (you love the hammer), not the plumbing.

The honest thing to tell you: **you have two different things to name, and you're trying to name both with one word.**

1. **The project** (runtime, actor model, WaveDB substrate, the loop) → this needs a *technical*, non-colliding name. **Athanor**, **Alembic**, **Confluence**, **Homunculus** all fit here.

2. **The persona** (what you call *me*, the voice, the hammer) → this is where "Friday" *wants* to live, and where it's actually fine as a *local, private* name — you can call your own local instance "Friday" on your own machine with zero legal risk, because that's not a product, it's a personal name.

The confusion is that you're asking "what do I name this project" while answering "what do I call my assistant."

---

## So here's the cleanest way out

**Decide which one you're naming right now.**

- If you're naming **the project** → **Athanor** (the alchemist's furnace, where the homunculi are made, and it's yours, public domain, in your Atomsk register, no collision). It's the *machine*.
- If you're naming **the assistant** → call it whatever you want — **Friday**, **the hammer**, **Misiques**, doesn't matter, because it's *your private local instance*, and "Friday" as the name of *your* personal assistant on *your* desktop is legally and practically fine. That's the persona, not the product.

The mistake you've been making is trying to make the *persona's name* do the job of the *product's name*. They're different things, and they've been different since message two when I told you the persona and the project are separate layers.

So: **Athanor** for the runtime, **Friday** for your local instance of the hammer. One is the furnace, one is the flame. Both yours. Neither a lawsuit.

Which one were you actually trying to name?

## Project context (read once, don't build yet)

We are building a portable agent runtime in C. The full vision is:

  one generic loop + isolated actors + a durable store (WaveDB) + a loadable persona.

The runtime is a LIBRARY (embeddable in any host: desktop, Pondr, CLI). It is
NOT a chatbot and NOT a coding-agent-specific tool. The line between "coding"
and "non-coding" agents is erased by giving every actor the same verb surface;
specialization is subtraction, not reconfiguration.

Full architecture layers (for orientation only — do NOT build these now):
  L0  WaveDB                storage substrate (already exists, do not touch)
  L1  unified log/tree      sessions as subtrees, events as seq ranges
  L2  frame/scope           each frame = subtree + surface API
  L3  the loop              observe -> reason -> act (amoral)
  L4  tool pipeline         pre->execute->post->result guardrails
  L5  persona + escalation  loadable text modules

THIS TASK IS ONLY THE CONCURRENCY PRIMITIVE THAT L2-L3 SIT ON.

## What to build now

An actor-model runtime in C, plus CPython subinterpreter integration, reusing
the CPython embedding/FFI code that already exists in the liboffs codebase.

The actor model is deliberately minimal — stolen from Pony's *concurrency
model only*, NOT its type system and NOT its garbage collector:

  - actor   = isolated state + a behavior table + an inbox
  - message = the ONLY way actors interact (an async function call / verb)
  - no shared heap, no data races (structural isolation only)

## Non-negotiable design decisions

1. C only. This is a portable library. No C++, no Rust.

2. Messages are TRANSIENT CONTROL, not data. A message is consumed on receipt
   and leaves no durable trace. Durability is NOT this layer's job (WaveDB's
   WAL does that later). Do NOT build a message store or log here.

3. One OS thread per actor (for now). No work-stealing, no fiber scheduler.
   We already have async/await in C (used in WaveDB); pure-C actors multiplexed
   over few threads is a LATER optimization. Python actors need their own
   thread anyway (per-interpreter GIL).

4. The Python runtime is LAZY. An actor that never runs code must never pay
   the cost of booting a subinterpreter. Boot on first EXECUTE, teardown on
   actor end.

5. Non-blocking. An actor must NEVER block on Python. The actor's message loop
   and the Python execution loop are two different threads with a handoff.

## Architecture spec

### Core structs (start here)

    typedef struct msg {
        uint32_t  type;      // behavior tag
        uint64_t  sender;    // reply-to actor id
        uint64_t  corr;      // correlation id (for async/await resume)
        void     *payload;   // ownership TRANSFERS with the message
    } msg;

    typedef struct mailbox {
        mtx_t  lock;
        cnd_t  cond;
        msg   *head, *tail;
        size_t count;
    } mailbox;

    typedef struct actor {
        uint64_t  id;
        mailbox   inbox;
        behavior *behaviors;  // type -> fn
        pyrt     *py;         // NULL until first EXECUTE
    } actor;

    typedef void (*behavior)(actor *self, msg *m);

### Scheduler

    void actor_loop(actor *a) {
        for (;;) {
            msg *m = mailbox_recv(a);      // block on cond
            a->behaviors[m->type](a, m);   // must not block long
        }
    }

### Python runtime (the interesting part)

    typedef struct pyrt {
        thrd_t        thread;
        PyThreadState *tstate;   // the subinterpreter's thread state
        mailbox       work;      // EXECUTE requests queued here
    } pyrt;

  - python thread: lazy-boot a subinterpreter, hold its thread state, loop:

  - actor NEVER touches pyrt directly, python NEVER touches actor inbox directly.
    The message is the only bridge, both directions.

### Python-facing module (message OUT)

are C callbacks that post messages to the owning actor's inbox:

    invoking Python again is not).

    message; the message owns them; receiver frees. Never hold a borrowed

read liboffs and determine what's reusable: interpreter boot, thread-state
management, the calling conventions, error handling.

## Out of scope (do NOT build these)

  - the frame tree / spawn-join semantics (just message types for now)
  - the seven-verb surface (read/write/inspect/execute/spawn/report/remember)
  - persona, the loop, the tool pipeline, escalation

## Milestone / acceptance criteria

Build a single runnable test that proves this:

If that works, the concurrency spine is done. Frames, subagents, and the verb
surface are all just more message types on the same loop.
